card.headline: Alert camel chewing cud, firm hump
card.look: A healthy camel holds its head high, watches you with bright clear eyes and chews its cud calmly, often while kneeling. Its hump is firm and upright, and its droppings are small, dry, firm pellets.
card.action: Learn what is normal for each of your camels and look at every animal daily, so you notice any change early and call the vet before a problem grows.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy one-humped camel (dromedary) looks, sounds and behaves like in Kenya and East Africa. Camels are tough and hide illness well, so many herders only notice a problem when it is already serious. If you know your camels' normal behaviour, droppings, hump size and temperature, you can spot trouble days earlier. Early action saves milk, calves and money, and it helps your vet treat the animal more successfully.
detail.cause: A camel stays healthy when its body, its food, its water and its surroundings are in balance. The camel is a pseudo-ruminant, which means it chews cud like a cow but has a three-part stomach instead of four. Microbes in the first stomach break down tough browse such as acacia, Salvadora (the 'toothbrush tree') and dry grasses. These microbes need steady feeding and enough salt and minerals to work well. Camels need much more salt than cattle, which is why pastoralists take herds to salty water points or salt licks. The hump is a store of fat, not water. In good seasons it fills up, and in the long dry season the camel burns that fat slowly, so the hump shrinks. The camel copes with heat in a special way. When water is short, it lets its body temperature rise during the hot day and cools down again at night, which saves sweat and water. Its kidneys make thick, small amounts of urine, and its gut pulls water out of droppings, which is why healthy droppings are dry. A camel can go many days without drinking, especially when it eats green browse, and then drink a very large volume in a few minutes without harm. Good health also depends on low parasite numbers (worms, ticks, mange mites and the blood parasites that cause surra, which is camel trypanosomiasis), a calm herd, and a body condition that is neither too thin nor too fat.
spread: A healthy herd stays healthy mainly through good management: enough browse, regular watering and access to salt or mineral licks.
Health can quickly be put at risk when new camels are brought in from markets without a quarantine period, because they may carry mange, surra, camel pox or brucellosis.
Sharing water points and night bomas with many other herds increases the chance of picking up infections and parasites.
Biting flies, such as horse flies and stable flies, increase during and after the rains and spread surra from sick camels to healthy ones.
Long treks, transport, overcrowding and sudden changes in feed are stress triggers that can weaken a normally healthy camel.
Drought, poor browse and lack of minerals slowly lower body condition and immunity, so diseases appear more easily at the end of the long dry season.
detail.atRisk: All camels benefit from daily observation, but some need closer attention. Young calves in their first months are the most fragile, because they depend on colostrum (the first thick milk) and milk, and they suffer quickly from diarrhoea, pneumonia and ticks. Heavily pregnant females and those in early lactation need good feed and water because pregnancy lasts about 13 months and milking drains their reserves. Breeding bulls lose condition during the rut, the mating season, because they eat less. In Kenya, camels in pastoral systems in Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo and Samburu face long dry seasons and long distances to water. Camels kept in semi-zero-grazing or peri-urban dairy units, for example around Isiolo, Nanyuki and Nairobi, face different risks: limited browse, crowding, fly build-up and feed that may be stored poorly. The period at the start of the long and short rains is important too, because biting flies and ticks increase and lush feed can upset digestion.

early: The camel is alert, holds its head and neck up, and turns its ears and eyes towards sounds and movement around it.
It chews cud for long periods every day, often while kneeling (couched) on its chest with the legs folded under, with a steady side-to-side jaw movement.
Droppings are small, firm, dry oval pellets that do not stick to the tail; calves still feeding mainly on milk normally pass softer, pasty droppings.
The hump is firm and stands upright, its size matching the season: fuller after good rains and smaller but still firm late in the dry season.
The eyes are bright and clear with no tears or crust, and the inner eyelid and gums are moist and pink.
The coat is clean, and the skin is soft and elastic with no crusts, bald itchy patches or lumps.
Body temperature follows a daily pattern: roughly 36–38 °C in a well-watered camel, rising to about 40 °C by late afternoon when water is short, then cooling at night.
At rest the camel breathes slowly and evenly, about 5–12 breaths per minute, and the heart beats about 40–50 times per minute.
It walks evenly with the herd, eats eagerly when browsing, drinks well at watering, and milking females keep steady milk yields.
advanced: The camel stops chewing cud or eats much less than usual, even when good browse is available.
It stands or lies apart from the herd, lags behind on the way to browse, or does not get up when the herd moves.
It lies flat on its side for long periods instead of resting couched on its chest; this is a serious warning sign in a camel.
Droppings become watery, very soft, bloody or foul-smelling in an adult, or stop completely.
The morning temperature is above about 38.5 °C, or any reading is above 40 °C, together with dullness or poor appetite.
The eyes look dull or sunken, tears run down the face, or there is thick discharge from the nose or eyes.
The hump collapses, leans or shrinks fast and ribs and hip bones show more than the season explains.
Breathing becomes fast, noisy or laboured, or the camel coughs, grinds its teeth or groans while lying down.
There is lameness, swelling of the legs, joints, lymph nodes or under the jaw, scabs on the lips and nostrils, or itchy, thickened, crusty skin.
Milk yield drops suddenly, the udder is hot or hard, or a pregnant female aborts or produces a weak calf.

lookalikes.name: Bull in rut (mating season)
lookalikes.howToTell: A breeding bull pushes a pink, balloon-like soft palate called the dulla out of the side of his mouth, froths, gurgles, grinds his teeth, splashes urine onto his tail and gives off a strong smell from glands behind the head. He eats less and may become aggressive. This is normal breeding behaviour, not choking or rabies, though he still needs careful handling. A bull with a dulla that keeps eating cud between displays and stays alert is usually just in rut. Signs outside the breeding season, drooling without the dulla, difficulty swallowing or paralysis need a vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: High afternoon temperature in the hot season
lookalikes.howToTell: When water is short, a healthy camel lets its temperature rise to about 40 °C by late afternoon and cools down overnight. This saves water and is normal. Take temperatures early in the morning when you want to check for fever. A camel that is hot in the cool morning, or hot and dull, off feed or breathing fast, may have a fever and should be seen by a vet.

lookalikes.name: Seasonal hair shedding
lookalikes.howToTell: Camels shed patches of old hair as the hot season begins, leaving uneven, thin-looking areas. The skin underneath is smooth, soft and not itchy. Mange, caused by mites, makes the camel rub and scratch, and the skin becomes thick, wrinkled, crusty and often smelly, starting around the head, neck, belly and inner legs. If you see itching and crusts, call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Not drinking for several days and dry droppings
lookalikes.howToTell: A healthy camel, especially on green browse, may go many days without drinking and normally passes very dry pellets. This is how it saves water. The worry is a camel that refuses water at the watering point when others drink, or has sunken eyes, skin that stays tented when pinched, and stops passing droppings. A pregnant female that lifts her tail when a bull comes near is also normal, as this is a known sign of pregnancy, not a sign of pain.

detail.diagnosis: A short home health check, done the same way each time, gives you a picture of what is normal for each camel. Start by watching from a distance before you disturb the herd: who is alert, who is chewing cud, who is standing alone, and how each animal walks. Then check the hump, ribs and hip bones to judge body condition; you should feel the ribs with light pressure but not see every rib sharply. Look at the eyes, nostrils, lips and mouth for discharge, sores or scabs. Run your hand over the skin of the neck, belly and legs for lumps, ticks, wounds or crusts, and gently feel under the jaw and in front of the shoulders for swollen lymph nodes. Check droppings in the boma and at resting places. For milking females, look at milk volume and check that the udder is soft and even. To take the temperature, couch the camel and hobble a front leg, with a helper holding the head rope. Lift the tail, insert a clean, lubricated digital thermometer gently into the rectum and press the tip against the side wall. Hold it until it beeps, then clean and disinfect it. Do this early in the morning for the most useful reading, and write it down. Count breaths by watching the flank rise and fall for one minute while the camel rests. You can feel or listen to the heart on the lower left chest behind the elbow. Keep a simple notebook of each camel's normal readings, body condition, milk yield, calving dates and treatments. If something looks wrong, your vet will use the same check plus blood smears for surra, blood tests for brucellosis, faecal tests for worms, skin scrapings for mange or milk tests for mastitis. Your notes will help the vet a great deal.
firstSteps: Look at every camel at least once a day, ideally when they leave the boma in the morning and when they return, and note any animal that is slow, alone or not chewing cud.
Take the morning temperature of any camel that looks dull, and compare it with its normal reading in your records.
Separate a camel that seems unwell from the herd, give it shade, water and fresh browse, and keep it calm and away from strangers' herds.
Stop moving, selling or buying camels from a group where an animal looks sick until a vet has checked it.
Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling sick animals, aborted calves, afterbirths or discharges, and boil milk from any camel that is unwell.
Write down what you saw, when it started, what the camel ate and drank, and any treatments given, then call your vet, a trained animal health worker or the County Veterinary Officer.

Do not give antibiotics, trypanocides or other drugs bought from the agrovet without a vet's advice, because wrong drugs or wrong amounts can hide disease, cause resistance and leave residues in milk and meat.
detail.vetTreatment: Healthy camels still benefit from routine vet care, planned with your vet or County Veterinary Officer for your area and season. Routine care often includes a yearly or seasonal herd check: body condition, teeth, feet, udders and breeding history. Parasite control is a big part of it. The vet can test droppings and decide when and with what to deworm, rather than dosing blindly, which helps slow drug resistance in worms. In areas with biting flies and tsetse, the vet may screen blood for surra and advise on trypanocidal drugs, which must be used correctly because the wrong product can harm camels. Ticks and mange mites are controlled with acaricides chosen by the vet for camels. Vaccine options for camels are fewer than for cattle and vary by country, so ask your vet which vaccines, such as camel pox, are available and advised in your county. Testing for brucellosis is important in milking herds, especially where milk is sold. The vet may also advise on mineral and salt supplements, calf care and colostrum, castration and identification such as ear tags or brands. If any drug is used, the vet will tell you the withdrawal period, which is how long you must wait before milk or meat is safe to use or sell. Follow it strictly. Use antibiotics only when a vet says they are needed, and finish the course as prescribed, because careless use creates resistant germs that harm both animals and people.
prevention: Give camels enough time on mixed browse each day, and when you must hand-feed, introduce new feeds slowly so the stomach microbes can adjust.
Provide regular access to salt, mineral licks or traditional salty water points, because camels have a very high salt need and lack of it lowers appetite and health.
Water camels on a regular schedule suited to the season and keep watering points as clean as possible, avoiding stagnant, dirty pools.
Make sure every newborn calf suckles colostrum within the first hours of life, keep calf pens clean and dry, and protect calves from ticks and cold nights.
Plan deworming, tick, mange and surra control with your vet, using tests where possible and keeping records of every product used.
Quarantine new or returning camels for a few weeks, watch them daily, and ask the vet to test them, for example for brucellosis and surra, before they join the herd.
Keep night bomas clean, dry and not overcrowded, and remove dung regularly to reduce flies, especially in dairy units near towns.
Store any concentrates or hay dry and off the ground so they do not go mouldy, and never feed mouldy feed.
Keep simple records of temperature, body condition, milk yield, breeding and treatments, so you can compare each camel with its own normal.
detail.impact: Healthy camels are the backbone of many households in northern and eastern Kenya. They give milk through long dry seasons when cattle and goats are struggling, and camel milk is increasingly sold in towns such as Isiolo, Garissa, Wajir and Nairobi. Camels also provide meat, transport, income from sales and social value in dowry and other traditions. Because camels breed slowly, with a pregnancy of about 13 months and usually one calf every two years or so, losing a breeding female or calf is a very large setback that takes years to recover from. Illness often shows first as a quiet drop in milk, slower growth or weight loss, long before an animal collapses. A farmer who checks the herd daily and knows normal signs can catch problems early. This keeps treatment costs lower, protects milk sales and reduces the risk that one sick camel infects the rest of the herd.
detail.humanHealth: Even camels that look completely healthy can carry germs that infect people. Brucellosis, a bacterial infection causing long-lasting fever and joint pain in people, can pass through raw camel milk and through contact with afterbirths and aborted calves. Camels in Kenya and the region have also been found to carry MERS coronavirus, a virus that can cause severe breathing illness in people, usually with no signs in the camel. To protect your family, boil or pasteurise camel milk before drinking, wash hands with soap after milking and handling camels, wear gloves when helping with calving or handling afterbirths, and cook camel meat thoroughly. Anyone who develops fever, cough or joint pain after close contact with camels should visit a health facility and mention their work with camels. Always respect drug withdrawal periods so that drug residues do not end up in milk or meat.
detail.outlook: Camels are hardy animals and can live and work for well over 20 years when they are well managed. A camel that is alert, chewing cud, keeping its hump and body condition for the season and passing firm dry droppings is usually in good health. The outlook for any camel depends on how quickly problems are spotted, how good the feed, water and mineral supply is, and how well parasites and infections are controlled. Camels hide illness, so changes can be small at first. Herders who check their animals daily, keep records and call the vet early are much more likely to keep a productive herd through droughts and disease seasons.

faqs.q: What is a normal temperature for a camel?
faqs.a: It changes with the time of day and how much water the camel has. A well-watered camel usually stays around 36–38 °C. When water is short in the hot season, a healthy camel can warm up to about 40 °C by late afternoon and cool down again overnight. This is normal and helps it save water. For checking fever, take the temperature early in the morning. A morning reading above about 38.5 °C, or any reading over 40 °C, together with dullness or poor appetite, is a reason to call the vet.

faqs.q: My camel's hump has become small. Is it sick?
faqs.a: Not always. The hump stores fat, and camels use it up during the long dry season, so it shrinks naturally when browse is poor. A healthy hump stays firm and upright even when smaller. Be concerned if the hump shrinks quickly, falls to one side or becomes floppy, or if the ribs and hip bones show a lot while other camels in the same herd still look fine. That can point to worms, surra, poor teeth or another illness, and a vet should check the camel.

faqs.q: How long can a healthy camel go without water?
faqs.a: It depends on the season, the heat, the work it does and the browse. On green browse in cooler weather, camels may go a long time without drinking, and in hot dry periods they need water more often. Milking females, pregnant camels and calves need water more regularly than other camels. Long water stress lowers milk yield and body condition, so even though camels can survive without water, regular watering keeps them productive.

faqs.q: Why is my bull camel blowing a pink bubble out of his mouth?
faqs.a: That pink balloon is the dulla, part of the soft palate that bulls push out during the rut, the breeding season. It comes with gurgling sounds, froth, teeth grinding, a strong smell and splashing urine on the tail. It is normal and not a sign of choking. Rutting bulls can be dangerous, so handle them carefully and keep children away. If you see drooling without a dulla, trouble swallowing, staggering or paralysis, call a vet immediately.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm and treat my camels?
faqs.a: There is no single schedule that suits every herd. It depends on your area, the season, the rains and the type of grazing. Ask your vet to test droppings and blood, and to plan worm, tick, mange and surra control for your herd. Treating only when needed, with the right product, saves money and slows drug resistance. Always follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods the vet gives you.

faqs.q: Do I need to give vitamins or supplements to healthy camels?
faqs.a: Camels on good mixed browse with access to salt and minerals usually get most of what they need. Late in the long dry season, when browse is dry and green feed is scarce, levels of vitamins such as vitamin A can fall. Stress such as long treks or transport in heat also drains camels. Talk to your vet or agrovet about whether a vitamin or rehydration product would help your herd at such times, and always follow the label. Supplements support good feeding, salt and parasite control but do not replace them.

products.role: During the late dry season, when green browse is scarce and vitamin A levels can drop, AD3E can help top up vitamins A, D3 and E for pregnant and milking camels. Use it alongside good browse, salt and minerals and routine vet care, following the label and your vet's advice.

Before and after long treks, transport or very hot periods, this oral rehydration solution can help camels replace fluids and electrolytes and cope with heat stress. It supports, but does not replace, regular watering, shade and calm handling.

card.headline: Shrinking hump and steady weight loss
card.look: The camel slowly gets thinner, the hump shrinks and sags, and the gums and eyes look pale. It is often dull, has runny eyes, and may show soft swelling under the belly, chest or lower legs.
card.action: Separate the sick camel, keep it in shade with water, and call a vet to take a blood sample for testing before any trypanocide is given.

detail.summary: Surra is a blood parasite disease of camels caused by Trypanosoma evansi, a tiny organism that lives and multiplies in the blood. Biting flies carry it from camel to camel. It is the most important disease of camels in Kenya and the Horn of Africa. It can kill quickly, but more often it drags on for months or even years, slowly wasting the camel, cutting milk yield and causing abortions.
detail.cause: Surra is caused by Trypanosoma evansi, a single-celled parasite called a trypanosome that swims in the blood and body fluids. Unlike the trypanosomes behind 'nagana' in cattle, it does not need tsetse flies; any biting fly that feeds on an infected camel and then quickly bites another can carry it on its mouthparts. Once inside, the parasites multiply in waves. Each wave brings a bout of fever, then the camel's immune system knocks the numbers down, then the parasites change their outer coat and multiply again. This is why the fever comes and goes. The parasites and the body's reaction to them destroy red blood cells, causing anaemia (too little blood to carry oxygen). The camel loses appetite, burns its fat reserves including the hump, and the liver and other organs are stressed. Low blood protein lets fluid leak out of the vessels, producing soft swellings (oedema) under the belly, brisket and legs. In pregnant camels the fever and anaemia can kill the unborn calf, leading to abortion or weak calves. Without treatment many camels slowly waste and die, often when another stress such as drought or a long trek is added.
spread: Horse flies (Tabanus, the large flies with a painful bite) are the main carriers; they bite, get disturbed, and finish their meal on the next camel, carrying blood and parasites with them.
Stable flies (Stomoxys) and camel flies (Hippobosca) also carry the parasite in the same way, especially when camels crowd together at water points and night bomas.
Fly numbers rise sharply during and after the long rains and the short rains, so new infections peak in the wet season and the weeks after it.
Grazing near rivers, swamps, riverine forest and thick bush, where biting flies breed, greatly increases the risk.
Reusing the same needle or syringe on several camels can carry infected blood from one animal to the next.
Moving camels into a new area, buying in animals from markets, and mixing herds at shared watering points bring infected camels into contact with healthy ones.
Chronically infected camels that look only slightly thin can carry the parasite for a long time and act as a hidden source for the rest of the herd.
detail.atRisk: Camels of all ages can get surra, but adult camels, pregnant and milking females, and working pack camels suffer most because they are under the most stress. Camels from dry areas with little fly challenge suffer badly when moved into wetter, bushier areas. Risk is highest during and after the long rains (March to May) and short rains (October to December), when biting flies are plentiful. Pastoral herds in northern and eastern Kenya, including Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Turkana and Laikipia, are heavily affected, as are herds that graze along rivers such as the Tana, Ewaso Ng'iro and Daua. Camels that are underfed, wormy, or stressed by drought, long treks or other illness are more likely to become seriously sick. Horses, donkeys and dogs can also be infected and may become very ill; cattle, goats and sheep usually get milder infections.

early: Bouts of fever that come and go: the camel feels hot, is dull and stands apart, then seems to recover for a few days before the next bout.
Runny, watery eyes and a slightly reduced appetite, often around the time of the fever.
Gradual weight loss even when grazing is fair, with the camel lagging behind the herd.
A drop in milk yield in lactating females.
Pale pink rather than healthy pink gums and inner eyelids, a first sign of anaemia.
Many herders notice a strong, unusual sweetish or sharp smell to the urine of infected camels; this is a useful warning sign but not proof on its own.
advanced: Obvious wasting with ribs and hip bones showing, and a small, soft or collapsed hump.
Very pale or whitish gums and eyelids, weakness, and tiring quickly when walking or loaded.
Soft swellings (oedema) under the belly, brisket, sheath or udder and on the lower legs that may pit when pressed with a finger.
Dull, rough coat and hair loss in patches.
Abortion, stillbirth or the birth of weak calves that do poorly.
Lying down for long periods, difficulty getting up, and in some cases staggering or other nervous signs.
Death, either suddenly in a severe acute attack or after a long, slow decline, often triggered by drought or another stress.

lookalikes.name: Heavy worm burden (especially Haemonchus, the barber's pole worm)
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms also cause pale gums, weight loss and bottle-jaw type swelling, but usually without bouts of fever. Several camels on the same grazing are often affected, and a faecal egg count at a lab will show many worm eggs. Surra is confirmed by finding trypanosomes or antibodies in a blood sample. The two often occur together, so a vet may test for both.

lookalikes.name: Starvation and drought stress
lookalikes.howToTell: In drought the whole herd loses condition together, the hump shrinks in all animals, and they pick up when rains and pasture return. Camels with surra lose weight even when feed is available, show fever and runny eyes, and keep wasting after the rains.

lookalikes.name: Brucellosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Brucellosis also causes abortion, but aborting camels usually stay in fair body condition without repeated fever, pallor or wasting. Brucellosis is diagnosed with a separate blood test and can infect people through raw milk and birth fluids, so handle all abortions with gloves.

lookalikes.name: Sarcoptic mange
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange camels lose condition and hair, but the main sign is intense itching, rubbing and thick, crusty, wrinkled skin, especially on the head, neck, flanks and legs. Surra causes patchy hair loss without the severe itching and crusts, and comes with pale gums and fever.

detail.diagnosis: Signs alone are not enough because many conditions cause wasting. A vet or animal health technician will check temperature, body condition, gum colour and swellings, then take blood. The simplest test is to look at a fresh drop of blood or a stained blood smear under the microscope for moving trypanosomes. Spinning blood in a thin tube (the buffy coat or haematocrit centrifuge test) concentrates the parasites and also measures the packed cell volume (PCV), which shows how anaemic the camel is. Because parasite numbers rise and fall, a negative smear does not rule surra out, especially in chronic cases. Labs can also use blood tests that detect antibodies, such as the card agglutination test (CATT/T. evansi) or ELISA, or a PCR test that finds the parasite's genetic material. In dead camels a post-mortem may show a thin carcass, pale tissues, watery fluid in body cavities and an enlarged spleen and lymph nodes, but blood tests on living herd mates are more useful. To help the vet, note when the fever bouts happened, which camels are thin or have aborted, where the herd has grazed and watered recently, any recent purchases or treks, and any drugs already given, with names and dates. Ideally have the camel sampled while it has a fever, when parasites are easiest to find.
firstSteps: Separate the sick camel from the herd where you can, and keep it in shade near the boma so it does not have to walk far.
Make sure it has easy access to clean drinking water and good-quality browse or fodder, because fever and anaemia sap its strength.
Stop loading, working or trekking the camel; extra exertion can make an anaemic camel collapse.
Protect it from biting flies as much as possible, for example by keeping it away from rivers and thick bush and resting it in an open, breezy spot at the hottest fly times.
Check the rest of the herd closely for thin animals, pale gums, runny eyes, swellings and recent abortions, and write down what you find.
Record the camel's temperature if you have a thermometer, the dates of fever bouts, and any treatment already given.
Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trained animal health worker to take blood samples before any drug is used.

Do not inject cattle trypanocides or any other drug without a vet's advice; camels react badly to some products and wrong doses cause poisoning and drug resistance. Use a new or properly sterilised needle for every animal.
detail.vetTreatment: Surra is treated with trypanocides, which are drugs that kill trypanosomes. They are not antibiotics, and antibiotics do not cure surra, though a vet may use them if there is a second bacterial infection. Drugs commonly used in camels include quinapyramine and melarsomine, which has been developed specifically for T. evansi in camels. Some trypanosome drugs used in cattle, such as diminazene and isometamidium, are riskier in camels, which are more sensitive to their toxic effects, so the choice of drug, the dose and the route must be decided by a vet for camels specifically. Some products can also be used preventively at the start of the fly season under veterinary guidance. Treatment must be prescribed by a vet; never borrow cattle doses. Injection site swelling, drooling, trembling or restlessness can occur with some drugs, so the camel should be watched after treatment. Most treated camels improve over days to weeks, but rebuilding the hump, body condition and blood takes longer and needs good feeding and rest. Resistance of T. evansi to trypanocides is a real and growing problem, driven by under-dosing, fake or poor-quality drugs and repeated use of the same product, so buy from licensed agrovets and follow the vet's plan. All trypanocides have milk and meat withdrawal periods, during which milk and meat must not be used for people; ask the vet for the exact period of the product used and keep to it.
prevention: Reduce fly contact: where possible, graze away from rivers, swamps and thick bush during and after the rains, and water camels at cooler times of day when biting flies are less active.
Ask your vet about fly control products that are approved for camels, such as pour-ons or sprays, and about fly traps or insecticide-treated targets near bomas and water points.
Under veterinary advice, consider preventive trypanocide treatment for high-risk herds before or at the start of the rainy season or before moving camels into fly-infested areas.
Check new camels before mixing them with your herd: keep them apart for a few weeks and have them blood-tested for surra.
Use one clean needle per camel for all injections and never share syringes between herds.
Keep camels in good body condition with access to browse, salt and minerals, and plan for drought, because well-fed camels cope with infection far better.
Control worms with a planned deworming programme agreed with your vet, since worms and surra together cause severe anaemia.
Watch the herd regularly for weight loss, pale gums, runny eyes and abortions, and have suspect camels tested early rather than waiting for them to waste.
Buy trypanocides only from licensed agrovets, use the full prescribed dose, and rotate products as your vet advises to slow down drug resistance.
detail.impact: For pastoral and commercial camel keepers in Kenya, surra is one of the biggest drains on income. Milk yield falls in sick females, and since camel milk is a key food and cash product in northern Kenya, families feel the loss quickly. Abortions and weak calves slow herd growth for years. Wasted camels fetch much lower prices at market, and pack and riding camels cannot work. Repeated drug purchases, transport to get treatment, and losses from deaths in severe or neglected cases add to the cost. Chronic carriers keep the disease circulating, so one untreated camel can cost the whole herd. Drug resistance makes treatment less reliable and more expensive over time.
detail.humanHealth: Surra is not considered an important disease of people, although a very small number of human infections with T. evansi have been reported worldwide. The main human concern is drug residues: camel milk is often drunk raw, and milk or meat from camels treated with trypanocides must not be consumed until the withdrawal period given by the vet is over. Because abortions in camels can also be caused by brucellosis, which does infect people, always wear gloves when handling aborted calves and birth fluids, bury or burn them, and boil camel milk before drinking.
detail.outlook: Camels diagnosed and treated early with an appropriate trypanocide usually recover well, although they need weeks of good feeding and rest to regain the hump and body condition. The outlook is more guarded in camels that have been sick for a long time, are severely anaemic, very thin, heavily pregnant or also carrying worms or other diseases. Relapses happen if the drug did not clear all the parasites, if the parasites are resistant, or if the camel is quickly reinfected by flies. Recovered camels can be infected again, so prevention and regular checks remain important.

faqs.q: My camels are far from tsetse areas. Can they still get surra?
faqs.a: Yes. Surra does not need tsetse flies. It is carried by common biting flies such as horse flies and stable flies, which are found across camel country, especially after the rains. That is why surra occurs throughout northern and eastern Kenya, even in dry areas.

faqs.q: Can I use the trypanosome injection I use for my cattle?
faqs.a: Not without a vet's advice. Camels are more sensitive than cattle to some trypanocides, and a cattle product or dose can poison a camel or fail to clear the infection. Using the wrong drug or too little of it also helps the parasite become resistant. Ask a vet which product is suitable for camels and how it should be given.

faqs.q: Is the strange smell of the urine enough to know my camel has surra?
faqs.a: The unusual urine smell that many herders recognise is a helpful warning, and it is worth taking seriously. But it is not proof, and other conditions can change urine smell. A blood test is the reliable way to confirm surra, so use the smell as a reason to call the vet, not as a replacement for testing.

faqs.q: Can we drink the milk from a camel with surra?
faqs.a: The parasite itself is not considered a real risk to people through milk, but sick camels give less milk and it should be boiled like all camel milk. The bigger concern is drugs: after a camel is treated with a trypanocide, its milk and meat must not be used until the withdrawal period stated by the vet has passed.

faqs.q: Why did my camel get sick again after being treated?
faqs.a: There are several possible reasons. The camel may have been reinfected by flies, the dose may not have been right, the drug may have been of poor quality, or the parasites in your area may be resistant to that drug. Tell your vet so they can retest the camel and, if needed, change the treatment and advise on fly control.

faqs.q: Can surra spread to my donkeys, horses, goats or dogs?
faqs.a: Yes, T. evansi can infect several animals. Horses, donkeys and dogs can become seriously ill, while cattle, goats and sheep usually have milder infections but can still carry the parasite. If other animals near your camels become thin, weak or feverish, ask the vet to test them too.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can help a feverish, weak camel keep drinking and stay hydrated in hot conditions while it receives vet-prescribed trypanocide treatment. It supports comfort and recovery only and does not kill the parasite.

Vitamins A, D3 and E can help support a camel recovering from surra whose body reserves have been run down, particularly after drought and weight loss, when advised by your vet as part of recovery feeding. It does not treat surra or replace trypanocides, fly control or good nutrition.

card.headline: Pox scabs on lips and nostrils
card.look: Raised red spots appear on the lips, nostrils and eyelids and turn into blisters, pus-filled bumps and then dark crusts. The camel often has a fever, watery eyes and swollen glands, and calves may become covered in lesions all over the body.
card.action: Separate the sick camel from the herd, keep its calf and other young camels away from it, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer.

detail.summary: Camel pox is a contagious viral skin disease of camels. It causes fever and pox lesions that start on the head and can spread over the whole body. Adult camels usually recover, but young calves can get a severe form and some die. It matters to herders because it cuts milk, slows growth, causes abortions, lowers market value and can occasionally infect the people who handle sick camels.
detail.cause: Camel pox is caused by the camelpox virus, an orthopoxvirus. Orthopoxviruses are a family of viruses that also includes cowpox and the old human smallpox virus. The virus enters through small breaks in the skin or the lining of the mouth and nose. It multiplies there and in nearby lymph nodes, which are the 'glands' under the jaw and in front of the shoulder, so they swell. It then travels in the blood and settles in the skin. Each lesion goes through stages over days: a red spot (macule), a raised bump (papule), a fluid blister (vesicle), a pus-filled bump (pustule), and finally a dry crust or scab that falls off and leaves a scar. In the mild form, lesions stay mostly on the lips, nostrils, eyelids and face. In the generalised form, lesions cover the neck, legs, belly, udder and genitals, and can also form inside the mouth, throat, airways and gut. This makes eating, drinking and breathing painful. Raw lesions easily become infected with bacteria, which causes much of the serious illness and many of the deaths. The scabs that fall off are full of virus and can stay infectious in the dry environment for a long time.
spread: Direct contact between a sick camel and a healthy one, especially nose-to-nose contact, licking and suckling, spreads the virus quickly.
Scabs that fall off sick camels contain a lot of virus and can stay infectious for months in dry, shaded places such as bomas, resting spots and under trees.
Shared water troughs, feeding places, ropes, saddles, halters and milking containers carry the virus from one camel to another.
Bringing in newly bought camels, or mixing herds at markets, water points and during migration, is a common way the disease enters a healthy herd.
Biting ticks, especially Hyalomma ticks, may be able to carry the virus between camels, although direct contact is the main route.
People's hands and clothing can carry virus from a sick camel to a healthy one, for example when one person milks the whole herd.
detail.atRisk: Young camels, usually under about three years old and especially calves still suckling, are most at risk of the severe, generalised form. Older camels that have never been exposed can also get sick, while camels that recovered before usually stay protected for a long time. Pregnant females may abort. Camels weakened by poor grazing, heavy worm or tick loads, or other illness tend to suffer more. Outbreaks are often reported during and after the rains, when herds gather at water points and fresh grazing and when movement and trading increase. In Kenya the disease matters most in pastoral camel areas such as Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Turkana, Samburu and Laikipia, and in herds where animals are bought and sold frequently.

early: Fever: the camel feels hot, seems dull and may stand apart from the herd or lie down more than usual.
Reduced appetite and less interest in browsing, and a lactating camel may give noticeably less milk.
Watery eyes and tears running down the face, sometimes with a runny nose.
Swollen, firm glands under the jaw, below the ear or in front of the shoulder that you can feel with your hand.
Small red spots on the lips, around the nostrils and on the eyelids that soon become raised bumps.
Swelling of the lips and face, and drooling in some animals.
advanced: Blisters and pus-filled bumps that break and form thick brown or dark crusts on the head, neck, legs, belly, udder, groin and around the tail.
In calves, lesions joining together over large areas of skin, with the calf becoming weak and thin very quickly.
Sores in the mouth and on the tongue that make the camel unable to eat or drink properly, and calves that refuse to suckle.
Difficult or noisy breathing and discharge from the nose when lesions reach the airways.
Swollen, crusted eyelids, cloudy eyes and sometimes blindness in one or both eyes.
Bad-smelling, pus-filled wounds when bacteria infect the lesions, and flies gathering on them.
Diarrhoea, dehydration and severe weight loss in calves with the generalised form.
Abortion in pregnant camels and, in severe cases, death, mostly among young calves.

lookalikes.name: Camel contagious ecthyma (orf-like disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is caused by a different virus (a parapoxvirus) and also mostly affects young camels. The thick, wart-like crusts usually stay on the lips, muzzle and around the mouth and rarely spread over the whole body, and fever is often mild. The two diseases can look very similar and can even occur together, so only a laboratory test on scabs can tell them apart for certain.

lookalikes.name: Camel papillomatosis (warts)
lookalikes.howToTell: Warts are firm, dry, cauliflower-like growths on the lips and face that grow slowly. There is no fever, no blister or pus stage, and the camel usually stays bright and eats well.

lookalikes.name: Mange (sarcoptic mange)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange causes intense itching, so the camel rubs and bites itself. You see hair loss and thick, wrinkled, crusty skin, often on the head, neck, flanks and inside the thighs, but no fever and no sequence of blisters turning into pustules. A vet can confirm it with a skin scraping.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (rain scald)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial skin infection appears in wet weather as tufts of matted hair that lift off like a paintbrush, leaving raw, moist skin underneath. It does not usually start on the lips, nostrils and eyelids, and the camel is rarely feverish.

detail.diagnosis: An experienced vet can often suspect camel pox from the typical lesions on the lips, nostrils and eyelids, the fever, the swollen glands and the way it spreads through young camels. Because contagious ecthyma and other skin diseases look similar, the vet may collect samples to confirm it. Useful samples are fresh scabs, fluid from unbroken blisters, and swabs from lesions, sometimes with a blood sample. These are sent to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary laboratory, where tests such as PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material) or virus isolation confirm the cause. If a calf dies, a post-mortem can show lesions in the mouth, airways and gut. You can help by writing down when the first animal got sick, how many camels and calves are affected, their ages, any deaths or abortions, recent purchases or herd mixing, and any treatments already given. Keep sick animals restrained in a shaded place where the vet can examine them safely.
firstSteps: Isolate every camel with fever or pox lesions in a separate shaded area, away from the rest of the herd and especially away from young calves and pregnant females.
Stop buying, selling, lending or moving camels from your herd, and keep the herd away from shared water points and markets where possible until the vet has seen it.
Wear gloves when you handle sick camels, wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards, and cover any cuts on your hands.
Make sure sick camels have easy access to clean water, shade and soft, palatable browse or fodder, because mouth sores make eating painful.
Help calves that cannot suckle well by gently offering milk or water, and watch them closely for weakness and dehydration.
Use separate ropes, buckets and milking containers for sick animals, and milk sick camels last so you do not carry the virus to healthy ones.
Collect fallen scabs and contaminated bedding and burn or bury them, and clean shared equipment.
Record which animals are sick, their ages and signs, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer; do not give antibiotics or other drugs unless a vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the camelpox virus, so treatment is supportive. This means helping the camel's own body fight the virus while preventing complications. Antibiotics do not cure camel pox; the vet uses them only to control bacterial infection of the sores, for example with broad-spectrum antibiotics such as oxytetracycline or penicillin-type drugs, chosen according to the case. Using antibiotics only when they are needed, for the full course the vet prescribes, helps prevent antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to drugs. The vet may also clean lesions with mild antiseptic solutions, apply soothing ointments or fly-repellent wound sprays, treat eye lesions to protect sight, and recommend vitamins and fluids for weak calves. Anti-inflammatory or fever-reducing medicine may be used in some cases. Any drug given to a camel can leave residues in milk and meat, so follow the withdrawal period your vet gives you before milk is drunk or sold or the animal is slaughtered. Many medicines have no withdrawal period specifically set for camels, so the vet will advise a safe waiting time. Most lesions dry and scab within one to two weeks and the whole illness often runs over about four to six weeks. Calves with the generalised form need close nursing and may still die despite good care.
prevention: Vaccination: live and inactivated camel pox vaccines exist and are used in several camel-keeping countries, and they give good protection. Availability in Kenya varies, so ask your County Veterinary Officer whether vaccine can be obtained and when to vaccinate young camels.
Quarantine newly bought camels for at least two to three weeks, away from your herd, and check them for fever and skin lesions before mixing them in.
Avoid buying camels from herds or markets where pox is known to be present, and limit mixing with other herds at water points during an outbreak where you can.
Control ticks and other parasites regularly with products and methods advised by your vet, because ticks may carry the virus and heavy parasite loads weaken camels.
Keep camels, especially calves and pregnant females, in good body condition with adequate browse, water and mineral supplements, because well-fed camels cope better with infection.
Clean bomas and resting areas, and collect and destroy scabs after an outbreak, because the virus can survive a long time in dry scabs.
Keep separate equipment for sick animals, and teach herders and milkers to wash their hands between animals.
Keep records of illness, purchases and vaccinations so that outbreaks can be traced and the vet can advise you better.
detail.impact: For a pastoral family, camels are milk, transport, savings and status, so camel pox hits hard. Sick lactating camels give much less milk, at the very time families depend on it. Calves can die or be stunted for months, which slows herd growth. Pregnant camels may abort, losing a whole year of production. Damaged skin lowers the value of hides, and visibly sick or scarred camels fetch lower prices or cannot be sold while the herd is affected. Extra labour is needed to nurse calves and keep sick animals apart, and vet visits, antiseptics and antibiotics add cost. Outbreaks can also disrupt marketing and movement between herds and counties.
detail.humanHealth: Camel pox can infect people, though this is uncommon. Herders, milkers and people who nurse sick camels have developed sore, pus-filled lesions on the hands and fingers, sometimes with mild fever and swollen glands in the armpit. Most human cases are mild and heal on their own, but anyone with a weak immune system, or any person who develops sores after handling sick camels, should visit a health centre and tell the health worker about the contact. To protect yourself, wear gloves when handling sick camels or their scabs, cover cuts and scratches, wash your hands well with soap and water, and do not let children play with sick calves. Do not drink raw milk from sick camels; boil all camel milk, and discard milk during the drug withdrawal period your vet gives you.
detail.outlook: Most adult camels recover within about four to six weeks, and recovered camels usually stay protected against the disease for many years. The outlook is much worse for young calves with the generalised form, especially when lesions reach the mouth and airways and they cannot suckle or breathe easily, and some will die. Recovery depends on the age and condition of the camel, how quickly bacterial infection of the sores is controlled, good nursing with water and soft feed, and fly control. Some camels are left with scars, and a few may lose sight in an eye. Pregnant females that abort will usually recover but lose that season's calf.

faqs.q: Can I drink milk from a camel that has camel pox?
faqs.a: It is safest not to drink raw milk from a sick camel. The virus can pass to people through contact, and sick camels often have lesions on the udder and teats. Boil any camel milk before drinking. If your vet has given the camel antibiotics or other drugs, throw the milk away for the whole withdrawal period they tell you, even if you boil it, because boiling does not remove drug residues.

faqs.q: Will a camel get camel pox again after it recovers?
faqs.a: Camels that recover from camel pox usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity, so they rarely get sick again. This is why the disease mostly affects young camels in herds where it is common. Camels from areas without the disease, or herds that have not been exposed for a long time, can still get sick at any age.

faqs.q: Is there a camel pox vaccine in Kenya?
faqs.a: Effective camel pox vaccines exist and are widely used in some Middle Eastern and Asian countries. Availability in Kenya can be limited and changes over time. Ask your County Veterinary Officer or a reputable agrovet whether a vaccine is available in your area and how it should be used for young camels.

faqs.q: Can camel pox spread to my goats, sheep or cattle?
faqs.a: Camelpox virus mainly infects camels, and goats, sheep and cattle are generally not affected. However, goats and sheep have their own pox and orf diseases that look similar, so if other animals on your farm develop skin lesions, ask your vet to check them rather than assuming they caught it from the camels.

faqs.q: Should I open or scrape off the scabs to help the camel heal?
faqs.a: No. Picking or scraping scabs makes the wounds raw, spreads the virus on your hands and invites bacterial infection and flies. Let the scabs dry and fall off naturally. Keep the area clean as your vet advises, and collect fallen scabs and burn or bury them so they do not infect other camels.

faqs.q: Can people really catch camel pox from camels?
faqs.a: Yes, but it is uncommon. Herders and milkers who handle sick camels have developed sores on their hands and fingers. These are usually mild and heal, but you should still wear gloves, cover cuts, wash your hands well and visit a health centre if you develop sores after handling sick camels.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help sick camels, and especially calves with mouth sores, fever or diarrhoea, replace lost water and salts when they are drinking and eating less. It supports recovery alongside vet care and good nursing and does not act against the virus.

Vitamins A, D3 and E support normal skin and mucous membrane health and general condition. This can help camels recovering from pox, particularly during dry seasons when browse is poor in vitamin A. Use it as your vet advises, as a nutritional aid alongside treatment, not as a cure.

card.headline: Thick, crusted, hairless itchy skin
card.look: The camel rubs and bites itself constantly against trees, posts and other camels. Patches of skin on the head, neck, flanks and inner thighs become bald, grey, crusty, wrinkled and thickened like old leather.
card.action: Separate itchy camels from the herd, wear gloves when handling them, and call your vet or animal health worker to confirm mange and plan treatment for the whole herd.

detail.summary: Mange in camels is a skin disease caused by a tiny mite, Sarcoptes scabiei, that burrows into the skin. It causes intense itching, hair loss and thick, crusted, cracked skin, starting on the head, neck, flanks and inner thighs and spreading over the body if left alone. It is one of the most common and costly skin problems of camels in the pastoral areas of northern and eastern Kenya and the Horn of Africa, because affected camels lose weight, give less milk and fetch lower prices. It also spreads easily to herders and milkers, causing itchy skin in people.
detail.cause: Camel mange is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. cameli, a mite too small to see clearly with the naked eye. The female mite digs tunnels (burrows) in the top layer of the skin, where she lays eggs. The eggs hatch, the young mites grow into adults within about two to three weeks, and the cycle repeats, so numbers build up fast on one animal. The burrowing, together with the mites' saliva and droppings, triggers a strong allergic-type reaction in the skin. This is why the itching is so severe. The skin responds by thickening, losing hair and forming crusts and scales. Constant rubbing, scratching and biting break the skin, producing cracks (fissures) that weep fluid and bleed slightly. These open cracks can become infected by bacteria and attract flies, which makes the skin worse. A heavily affected camel spends so much time scratching and is so uncomfortable that it browses less and rests poorly, so it loses body condition and milk. In young or already weak camels, widespread mange combined with poor nutrition and secondary infection can lead to severe wasting and occasionally death.
spread: Direct body contact between camels is the main route, especially when animals are crowded together in night enclosures (bomas), at water points, at markets and during treks.
Mites can survive for a short time off the animal, so shared rubbing trees, fence posts, resting grounds and walls of night enclosures can pass mites from one camel to the next.
Saddles, pack frames, harnesses, ropes, blankets and mats used on an infected camel and then on a healthy one can carry mites.
Bringing in a newly bought camel, or mixing herds at shared grazing, wells and markets, is a common way the disease enters a clean herd.
Mothers pass mites to their calves through close contact during suckling and resting.
Poor body condition, stress, heavy work and long dry spells do not cause mange on their own, but they weaken the skin's defences so mites multiply faster and disease becomes severe.
detail.atRisk: All camels can get mange, but young camels, weaned calves, old animals and any camel in poor body condition suffer the worst disease. Pregnant and heavily lactating she-camels, and pack or transport camels that work hard and carry saddles, are also at higher risk. Mange problems tend to rise during long dry seasons and cooler months, when grazing is poor, camels are weak and herds crowd together at the few remaining water points and in enclosures at night. Pastoral and agro-pastoral herds in Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu and similar areas, where herds mix at wells and markets, are commonly affected. Herds that buy in camels without a quarantine period, or that share grazing with infected herds, are more likely to be hit. Once mange is in a herd, untreated carrier animals keep reinfecting the others.

early: Frequent rubbing of the head, neck and body against trees, posts, walls or other camels, and biting or nibbling at the skin.
Restlessness, especially at night, with the camel getting up and lying down more often than usual.
Small raised bumps, redness and fine scaling on the face, around the eyes and lips, on the neck, flanks, inner thighs, belly, udder or around the genitals.
Thinning hair and small bald patches where the camel has been rubbing, often with grey, dandruff-like flakes.
Itching that gets worse when the camel is warm, for example after resting in the sun or after a trek.
advanced: Large bald areas with very thick, wrinkled, grey or dark skin that feels hard and leathery, sometimes covering most of the body.
Heavy yellow-grey crusts and deep cracks in the skin that may ooze clear fluid, bleed slightly or smell bad when infected.
Flies gathering on raw, broken skin, and sometimes wounds from the camel rubbing itself on thorny trees.
Weight loss, a visible drop in hump size, poor appetite and a dull, tired look, because the camel spends its energy scratching instead of browsing.
Marked fall in milk yield in lactating she-camels, and calves that stop growing well.
Pack camels that cannot carry a saddle because the skin under it is sore, cracked or infected.
In very weak or young camels, severe wasting, weakness and occasionally death, usually when mange is combined with hunger and other infections.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (dermatophytosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm is a fungal infection that makes round, well-defined grey or white crusty patches, mostly on the head, neck and shoulders of young camels. It is usually much less itchy than mange, and the patches are round and separate rather than spreading, thickened and wrinkled. A vet can tell them apart with skin scrapings and hair samples.

lookalikes.name: Camelpox
lookalikes.howToTell: Camelpox causes fever and pock-like lumps that turn into blisters and scabs, starting on the lips, nostrils, eyelids and then the legs, udder and body. Affected camels, especially young ones, are clearly sick with fever and swollen glands. Mange does not cause fever on its own and is mainly intense itching with thick, hairless skin.

lookalikes.name: Contagious ecthyma (camel orf)
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf mainly affects young camels and causes thick, warty scabs on the lips, mouth corners and nostrils, which can stop them suckling or browsing. It rarely spreads over the body, flanks and thighs the way mange does, and itching is not the main feature.

lookalikes.name: Lice and heavy tick infestation
lookalikes.howToTell: Lice and ticks can also cause rubbing and hair loss, but you can see them with your eyes: lice and their eggs (nits) stuck to hairs, or ticks attached around the ears, tail, udder and between the legs. Sarcoptic mites are too small to see and live inside the skin, which becomes very thick and crusted.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or trained animal health worker will usually suspect mange from the typical intense itching and the pattern of thick, crusted, hairless skin starting on the head, neck, flanks and inner thighs. To confirm it, they take deep skin scrapings: they gently scrape the edge of an active lesion with a blade until the skin just starts to show tiny pinpoint spots of blood, then look at the scrapings under a microscope for mites, eggs or mite droppings. Mites can be hard to find, so several scrapings from different places may be needed, and a negative result does not fully rule out mange. Sometimes the vet confirms the diagnosis by how well the herd responds to anti-mite treatment. They will also look for other causes of skin disease such as ringworm, camelpox, orf, lice and ticks, and check for secondary bacterial infection. Before the vet comes, the farmer can help by keeping suspected camels tied or penned apart, counting how many animals are itching, noting when the itching started, which camels were recently bought or mixed with other herds, what treatments have already been tried (including traditional remedies), and whether any family members or herders have developed an itchy rash.
firstSteps: Separate camels that are itching or have crusty, hairless skin from the rest of the herd, and keep them in their own resting area and away from shared rubbing trees as far as possible.
Protect yourself: wear gloves and long sleeves when handling affected camels, wash your hands and arms with soap and water afterwards, and change and wash clothes that touched the skin.
Stop sharing saddles, pack frames, ropes, mats and blankets between affected and healthy camels, and set aside equipment used on sick animals until it can be cleaned.
Check every camel in the herd carefully, including calves, looking at the head, neck, flanks, inner thighs, udder and genitals, and write down which animals show signs.
Make sure affected camels have easy access to water, shade and the best grazing or browse you can find, because weak, hungry camels suffer far worse mange.
Rest working or pack camels with skin lesions, especially where the saddle sits, so the skin is not rubbed further.
Avoid putting used engine oil, battery acid, diesel, strong detergents or other harsh substances on the skin; these can burn the skin, poison the camel and contaminate milk and meat.

Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trained animal health worker to confirm the problem and plan proper treatment for the whole herd, and do not sell or move itchy camels to markets until they are treated.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet, who will choose the product, the dose and how often to repeat it based on the camels' weight, condition and whether they are being milked. The commonly used treatments are anti-parasite drugs from the macrocyclic lactone group, such as ivermectin or doramectin, usually given by injection, and acaricides (mite- and tick-killing chemicals) such as amitraz, certain pyrethroids or organophosphates, applied as a spray or wash over the whole body. Because mite eggs are not always killed, treatment almost always has to be repeated after an interval set by the vet, and the whole herd, not just the visibly sick camels, should be treated at the same time to stop reinfection. Before spraying, the vet may advise soaking and softening thick crusts so the product reaches the mites. Where the cracked skin has become infected, the vet may add an antibiotic; antibiotics do not kill mites and should only be used when truly needed, exactly as prescribed, to reduce the risk of antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to medicines). Withdrawal periods are very important with these drugs: this is the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be used for people. Many anti-mite products are not approved for animals producing milk for human use, or have long withdrawal times, and camel milk is a daily food for many pastoral families, so tell the vet which camels are being milked. Expect itching to ease over one to several weeks after effective treatment, while hair regrowth and the skin returning to normal take much longer, often a few months in severe cases. Very weak camels may also need better feeding and supportive care to recover.
prevention: Quarantine newly bought camels or camels returning from markets and long treks for a few weeks, check them carefully for itching and crusty skin, and have them treated by a vet before they join the herd if needed.
Treat the whole herd when mange is diagnosed, follow the full repeat treatment the vet recommends, and recheck the herd afterwards so no carrier animals are left to reinfect the others.

Keep camels in good body condition with the best browse and grazing available, access to water and salt or mineral licks, especially before and during long dry seasons, because well-fed camels resist mange better.
Avoid overcrowding in night enclosures where possible, and give sick and healthy camels separate resting places.
Do not share saddles, pack frames, harnesses, ropes and blankets between camels without cleaning them; wash them and leave them in strong sun to dry before reuse.
Reduce mixing with herds known to have mange at wells, grazing areas and markets, and agree with neighbouring herders on treating at the same time where mange is widespread.
Include regular skin checks in your routine herd inspections, looking closely at the head, neck, thighs, udder and genitals, so mange is caught early when it is easier to control.
Keep good records of which camels were treated, with what, when, and the withdrawal dates for milk and meat, and plan routine parasite control with your vet or County Veterinary Officer.
detail.impact: Mange causes real losses for camel keepers. Itchy camels browse less and rest poorly, so they lose weight and condition, and she-camels give noticeably less milk, which hits household food and milk sales directly. Calves from affected mothers grow slowly and weak young camels may die when mange is combined with drought and hunger. Camels with thick, scarred skin and bald patches fetch lower prices at livestock markets, and their hides are damaged and worth less. Pack and transport camels may be unable to carry saddles for weeks, interrupting water carrying, trade and migration. There are also extra costs for drugs, vet services and labour, often for repeated treatments of the whole herd, and lost milk during withdrawal periods. Because the mites spread to people, herders and milkers can suffer itchy rashes that affect their sleep and work.
detail.humanHealth: Camel mange mites can spread to people who handle, milk, ride or sleep close to affected camels. In people the mite usually causes very itchy red bumps and small blisters on the arms, hands, chest, belly and legs where they touched the camel. This form from animals usually does not settle permanently on people and tends to fade once contact with infected camels stops and the herd is treated, but the itching can be severe and the skin can become infected from scratching. To protect yourself and your family, wear gloves and long sleeves when handling itchy camels, wash with soap and water after contact, wash clothes and bedding that touched affected camels, and keep children from playing with or sleeping beside them. Anyone with an itchy rash after working with camels should visit a health facility and mention the contact with mangy camels. Also respect milk and meat withdrawal periods after anti-mite drugs, so that drug residues do not end up in the family's food.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for most camels when mange is caught early and the whole herd is treated properly, with repeat doses as advised by the vet. Itching usually eases within weeks of effective treatment, although hair and skin may take a few months to look normal again, and badly scarred skin may stay thicker. Recovery is slower and less certain in camels with widespread, long-standing mange, deep infected cracks, very poor body condition, or other diseases at the same time, and some severely affected young or weak camels may not survive. Reinfection is common if only some camels are treated, if treatment is stopped early, if new camels are brought in without checks, or if the herd keeps mixing with infected herds. Good nutrition and consistent herd-wide control make the biggest difference to long-term success.

faqs.q: Can I use used engine oil or diesel to treat mange in my camels?
faqs.a: This is a common traditional practice, but it is not recommended. Engine oil and diesel can burn and irritate already damaged skin, they can be absorbed and poison the camel, and they contaminate milk, meat and hides. They may soften crusts and smother some mites, but they do not reliably clear the infestation, so mange usually comes back. Ask your vet or animal health worker for a proper anti-mite treatment and a plan for the whole herd.

faqs.q: Why do I need to treat camels that are not itching yet?
faqs.a: Mites spread quietly from camel to camel before you see signs, so animals that look healthy may already be carrying them. If you treat only the visibly sick camels, the hidden ones keep reinfecting the herd and you end up treating again and again. Treating the whole herd at the same time, and repeating treatment as the vet advises, gives the best chance of breaking the cycle.

faqs.q: Can my family still drink milk from a camel being treated for mange?
faqs.a: Not always. Many anti-mite drugs pass into milk, and some are not approved for animals producing milk for people or have long withdrawal periods. Always tell the vet which camels are being milked so they can choose a suitable product and tell you exactly how long to throw away the milk. Respect that time fully, even though it means losing milk for a while.

faqs.q: I have an itchy rash after milking a mangy camel. Did I catch it from her?
faqs.a: Quite possibly. Camel mange mites can cause itchy red bumps on people, especially on the arms, hands and chest. It usually settles once the camels are treated and you avoid close contact with infected animals, but you should visit a health facility for advice and to make sure scratching has not caused infection. Wear gloves and long sleeves and wash well after handling camels until the herd is clear.

faqs.q: How long until my camel's hair grows back?
faqs.a: Itching often improves within one to a few weeks of effective treatment, but the skin needs time to heal. Hair regrowth and softening of thick skin usually take a couple of months or longer in bad cases, and some scarred skin may never look completely normal. If itching continues or new crusts appear after the full course, call the vet back, because treatment may need adjusting or the camel may have been reinfected.

faqs.q: Will one injection cure my camel of mange?
faqs.a: Usually not. Treatments do not always kill mite eggs, so new mites hatch after the first treatment. Vets therefore normally repeat treatment after a set interval and treat all camels in the herd together. Follow the full plan your vet gives you, and keep affected camels well fed and watered, which helps their skin recover.

products.role: Vitamin A helps keep skin healthy, and vitamins A, D3 and E support general condition. In thin or poorly fed camels recovering from mange, a vet may use AD3E to help correct vitamin shortfalls and support skin repair. It does not kill mites and does not replace the vet's anti-mite treatment, good feeding or herd-wide control.
