mange.seoDescription: Camel mange (upele): spot thick, crusted, hairless itchy skin on head, neck and thighs. Learn first steps, vet treatment, prevention and herder safety.

card.headline: Crusted sores and lumps on neck, shoulders
card.look: Round, hairless swellings appear on the neck, shoulders or flanks. They soften, burst and leave raw, crusted or dead-looking sores that may ooze yellow pus, often with swollen glands nearby.
card.action: Separate the affected camel, keep flies and other camels away from the sores, and call your vet before the lesions spread through the herd.

detail.summary: Contagious skin necrosis is a bacterial skin disease of camels. Lumps and abscesses (pockets of pus) form in the skin, burst, and leave patches of dead skin (necrosis) that heal slowly. It is common in pastoral camel herds in northern and eastern Kenya, especially in the dry season. It rarely kills, but it costs milk, body condition, hide value and working ability, and it can spread through a herd if not managed.
detail.cause: The disease is mainly caused by bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus. Streptococcus bacteria, including Streptococcus agalactiae, are also often found in the sores, and other germs such as Dermatophilus congolensis may join in. These bacteria live on skin and in the environment. They usually cannot get through healthy, unbroken skin. Trouble starts when the skin is damaged by thorns, tick bites, biting flies, rubbing saddles or ropes, branding or fighting. The bacteria enter the small wound and multiply under the skin. The body sends white blood cells to fight them, and pus builds up, forming a firm, painful lump. As the lump grows, it cuts off blood supply to the skin above it, so that skin dies, turns dark or leathery, and peels or sloughs away. This leaves an open, weeping ulcer that slowly fills in and scars. The infection drains to the nearest lymph nodes (the glands that filter infection), which swell. Poor nutrition makes everything worse: camels short of salt, minerals such as calcium, phosphorus and zinc, and vitamin A in a long dry season have weaker skin and weaker immunity, so sores appear more easily and heal more slowly.
spread: Direct contact between camels, especially when they rub necks and shoulders together in crowded night enclosures (bomas) or at watering points.
Shared equipment such as saddles, saddle pads, halters, ropes and grooming tools carry pus from one camel to the next.
Thorny browse such as Acacia and Balanites scratches the neck and shoulders while camels feed, opening the skin to bacteria.
Ticks and biting flies damage the skin and may carry bacteria from sore to sore; flies are attracted to open, weeping lesions.
Pus and scabs that fall onto the ground, fences and resting places contaminate the environment for other camels.
Poorly done branding, ear-marking or traditional firing leaves wounds that can become infected.
Stress from long treks, heavy loads, drought, hunger and mineral shortage lowers resistance and triggers outbreaks.
detail.atRisk: Camels of all ages can be affected, but young camels and those around one to four years old are often reported to be hit harder, along with weak, thin or recently weaned animals. Pack and working camels that carry saddles and loads are at risk on the hump, withers and shoulders where equipment rubs. The disease is most common in pastoral systems in counties such as Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu and parts of Laikipia, especially in the hot dry season when browse is thorny and dry, salt licks are far away, ticks are plentiful and camels are crowded at few water points. Herds that are not given salt or mineral supplements, have heavy tick burdens, or share equipment between many animals have more cases.

early: Small, firm, painful swellings or nodules the size of a pea to a walnut on the neck, shoulders, withers, chest or flanks.
Patches where the hair stands up, falls out or looks matted over a swelling.
Swellings that feel warm and that the camel flinches from when touched.
The camel rubs or scratches the area against trees, fences or other camels.
Glands (lymph nodes) near the sores, such as in front of the shoulder, start to feel enlarged.
advanced: Lumps become soft in the centre, then burst and release thick yellow, cream or blood-tinged pus.
The skin over the lump dies, turning dark, dry and leathery, then peels away leaving a raw, weeping ulcer.
Sores join together into large crusted areas of damaged skin, sometimes over much of the neck and shoulder.
Clearly swollen, firm lymph nodes that may themselves form abscesses.
Flies gather on the sores, and maggots (myiasis) may appear in neglected wounds with a foul smell.
Weight loss, reduced feeding and lower milk yield in badly affected camels.
Occasional fever and dullness when infection is widespread, and scarred, thickened skin after healing.

lookalikes.name: Camelpox
lookalikes.howToTell: Camelpox is a viral disease that causes many small raised spots that turn into blisters and scabs, often starting on the lips, nostrils and eyelids and spreading over the body, usually with fever and more severe illness in young camels. Contagious skin necrosis usually starts with fewer, larger lumps on the neck and shoulders that fill with pus. A vet may need samples to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Mange (sarcoptic mange)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange is caused by tiny mites. It brings intense itching, hair loss and thick, wrinkled, crusty skin, often starting on the head, neck, inner thighs and belly, without the deep pus-filled lumps. A vet confirms it with a skin scraping under the microscope.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (dermatophytosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm is a fungal infection that causes round, grey, scaly, hairless patches, often on the head and neck of young camels. The patches are dry and flaky and do not usually form pus-filled lumps or swollen glands.

lookalikes.name: Caseous lymphadenitis
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a different bacterial disease (Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis) where the lymph nodes themselves form large abscesses with thick, cheesy pus, often without the spreading skin sores. Laboratory culture of the pus is the reliable way to tell the difference.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects contagious skin necrosis from the typical pattern: lumps and necrotic sores on the neck and shoulders, swollen glands, and a history of thorny browse, ticks or saddle rubbing in the dry season. To confirm it and choose the right treatment, the vet may take a swab or a sample of pus from an unopened abscess and send it to a laboratory, such as a County or regional veterinary laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, for bacterial culture and an antibiotic sensitivity test, which shows which drugs will work against the germs found. Skin scrapings may be taken to rule out mange, and scabs or tissue samples may be tested if camelpox or other diseases are possible. You can help by noting when the sores first appeared, how many camels are affected and their ages, any recent treks, new animals, tick problems or changes in grazing, whether salt or minerals are being given, and any treatments already used. Do not burst or treat lumps before the vet sees them, as this can spoil samples.
firstSteps: Separate affected camels from the rest of the herd and keep them in their own enclosure or tethered apart, especially at night and at watering points.
Do not share saddles, pads, ropes or halters between sick and healthy camels; set aside equipment used on the sick camel.
Wear gloves or cover your hands when touching sores, avoid contact with pus, and wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards.
Keep flies off the sores as far as you can, for example by keeping the camel in shade away from dung heaps and removing soiled bedding, so maggots do not get into the wounds.
Do not squeeze, cut or burn the lumps yourself; wrong opening or traditional firing can push infection deeper and leave large scars.
Make sure the camel has easy access to clean water, shade and good browse, and offer salt if it is normally given.
Check the whole herd carefully, feeling the neck and shoulders for early lumps, and write down which animals are affected.
Call your vet or the nearest veterinary officer and describe the sores, numbers affected and any fever or weight loss.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how many sores there are and how deep they go. For ripe abscesses, the vet will usually open them at the lowest point with clean instruments to let the pus drain, then flush the cavity and clean the sores with an antiseptic such as dilute iodine (povidone-iodine) or chlorhexidine. Dead skin may be gently removed so healthy tissue can heal. Antiseptic or antibiotic sprays and ointments are often applied to open sores, together with a fly repellent or wound spray to prevent maggots. Where many sores are present, glands are badly swollen or the camel has a fever, the vet may prescribe antibiotics given by injection. Drug classes commonly used include penicillins, tetracyclines such as oxytetracycline, and sometimes other groups chosen after a sensitivity test, because Staphylococcus bacteria can be resistant to some antibiotics. Only use antibiotics prescribed by a vet, give the full course exactly as directed, and never use leftover or shared drugs, because incomplete or wrong use breeds antibiotic-resistant bacteria that are harder to treat in camels and people. Very few drugs are tested and labelled specifically for camels, so vets set cautious milk and meat withdrawal periods (the time after treatment before milk or meat is safe to use); follow these strictly and ask your vet how long to keep milk out of the food chain. The vet may also treat for ticks and advise salt, mineral and vitamin supplements to help healing. Expect sores to take several weeks to heal, and some camels need repeat cleaning visits.
prevention: Provide salt and a good camel mineral supplement regularly, especially in the dry season, as mineral shortage is closely linked to outbreaks.
Control ticks with a regular programme advised by your vet or extension officer, and check the neck, shoulders and under the tail often.
Look after saddles and pads: keep them clean, well padded and fitted, rest camels with rubs, and do not move equipment from sick to healthy animals.
Treat any thorn scratches, branding marks or small wounds early by cleaning them and protecting them from flies.
Avoid overcrowding in night bomas and at watering points where camels rub against each other, and clean resting areas of pus and scabs.
Isolate new or returning camels for a few weeks and check their skin before mixing them with the herd.
Isolate camels with sores as soon as you see them so the disease does not spread through contact.
Keep camels in good body condition through careful grazing management and planned movements in drought, as strong camels resist infection better.
detail.impact: Contagious skin necrosis rarely kills camels, but it quietly drains income. Painful sores and fever reduce feeding, so camels lose condition and milk yield drops, which matters greatly in pastoral homes where camel milk is a main food and a growing cash income in markets such as Isiolo, Garissa and Nairobi. Milk from treated camels must be held back during withdrawal periods. Pack and working camels cannot carry saddles over neck and shoulder sores, so trade and transport work stops. Scarred skin lowers hide value, and camels with visible sores fetch lower prices at livestock markets or are refused by buyers. Treatment, repeated cleaning, transport to the vet and supplements add cost, and an outbreak that runs through young stock can set back herd growth.
detail.humanHealth: The bacteria involved, especially Staphylococcus aureus, can infect people through cuts and scratches on the hands, causing boils, skin infections and occasionally more serious illness. Some strains are resistant to common antibiotics. Wear gloves or cover your hands when handling sores or pus, wash well with soap afterwards, and keep children away from sick camels. Burn or bury dressings, scabs and pus-soaked material. If a camel has sores on or near the udder or shows signs of mastitis, do not drink its milk. Camel milk is often drunk raw in pastoral areas; boiling milk kills these bacteria and is strongly advised. After any antibiotic treatment, keep milk and meat out of human food until the vet's withdrawal period has passed, because drug residues can cause allergic reactions and add to antibiotic resistance.
detail.outlook: Most camels recover well when sores are cleaned, drained and protected early and nutrition is improved, although healing often takes several weeks and scars may remain. Recovery is slower in thin, young or mineral-deficient camels, in those with many joined-up sores or badly swollen glands, and where flies and maggots get into wounds. Cases can become long-lasting or keep returning if ticks, saddle rubs, thorns and mineral shortage are not dealt with. Early action and herd-wide prevention give the best results.

faqs.q: Can I just burst the abscess myself and put on engine oil or ash?
faqs.a: Please do not. Opening a lump at the wrong time or with dirty tools can push infection deeper, and engine oil, ash or hot irons damage the skin further and slow healing. They also do not kill the bacteria reliably. Let the vet open ripe abscesses cleanly, flush them and advise on safe wound care and fly control.

faqs.q: Why does this disease seem worse in the dry season?
faqs.a: In the dry season camels browse more thorny bushes, ticks and biting flies are often heavy, salt and minerals are scarce, and camels crowd at few water points. Damaged skin, poor nutrition and close contact together give the bacteria an easy way in. Giving salt and minerals and controlling ticks before the dry season helps a lot.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from a camel with these sores?
faqs.a: If the sores are only on the neck or shoulders and the camel is not on any drugs, boiled milk is generally considered safe, but hygiene during milking is important. Do not use milk from a camel with sores on the udder or signs of mastitis, and never use milk during the withdrawal period after antibiotic treatment. Always boil camel milk before drinking.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure it quickly?
faqs.a: Antibiotics help in some cases, but they work best alongside cleaning and draining the sores, and only if the right drug is used for the full course. Many camel cases need little or no injected antibiotic if wounds are well managed. Buying and using antibiotics without a vet risks the wrong drug, the wrong amount, resistant bacteria and drug residues in milk and meat. Let your vet decide.

faqs.q: Can my goats, sheep or cattle catch it from the camels?
faqs.a: The same types of bacteria can cause skin infections and abscesses in other livestock, so it is sensible to keep sick camels and their equipment away from other animals and to clean shared enclosures. Good hygiene and tick control protect the whole homestead.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for contagious skin necrosis?
faqs.a: There is no widely used commercial vaccine for this disease in camels in Kenya. Prevention depends on good nutrition with salt and minerals, tick and fly control, well-fitted clean saddles, quick care of small wounds and isolating affected camels early. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer about local advice.

products.role: Vitamin A helps keep skin healthy and supports healing and immunity, and camels in a long dry season with poor browse can run short of it. Where a vet agrees, AD3E can be used as a supportive supplement alongside wound care, any prescribed treatment and good mineral feeding. It does not treat the infection itself.

card.headline: One udder quarter swollen and hot
card.look: One quarter of the udder is larger, firmer and warmer than the others, and the camel may kick or refuse to let the calf suckle. Milk from that teat may be watery, yellowish, clotted, flaky or blood-tinged, or it may look normal.
card.action: Milk the affected quarter last into a separate container, throw that milk away safely, and call your vet or animal health officer the same day.

detail.summary: Mastitis is an infection and swelling of the udder, usually caused by bacteria that enter through the teat openings. In camels it is one of the most common causes of lost milk, and much of it is hidden: many camels have subclinical mastitis, where the milk looks normal but the quarter is infected and producing less. Because camel milk is a major food and income source in northern and eastern Kenya, and is often drunk raw, mastitis affects family nutrition, milk sales and human health at the same time.
detail.cause: Mastitis is caused mainly by bacteria. The most common in camels include Staphylococcus aureus and other staphylococci, streptococci (including Streptococcus agalactiae), and gut bacteria such as E. coli that come from dung and dirty ground. A camel's teat is unusual: each teat has two or sometimes three small openings (streak canals) instead of one, which gives bacteria more ways in. Bacteria get into the teat through dirty hands, dirty milking containers, the calf's mouth, flies, or damaged teat skin. Once inside, they multiply in the milk-producing tissue. The camel's body sends white blood cells to fight them, which causes heat, swelling, pain and changes in the milk such as clots and flakes. If the infection is strong, the tissue is damaged, scar tissue forms and the quarter may permanently produce less milk or dry up completely (a 'blind' quarter). Some bacteria, especially E. coli, can release toxins that make the whole camel sick with fever and weakness. Ticks are a special problem in camels: the large Hyalomma ticks often attach on and around the udder and teats, and their bites cause wounds, swelling and teat damage that let bacteria in. Traditional anti-suckling methods, such as tying teats with string or covering the udder with tight cloth or thorn-stick devices to stop the calf suckling, can also injure teats and trap dirt and milk, which raises the risk.
spread: Dirty hands of the milker carry bacteria from one infected camel to the next, especially when the same person milks the whole herd without washing.
Shared milking containers, cloths and towels that are not cleaned between camels spread bacteria, particularly Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.
The calf suckles before and during milking to help milk let-down, and a calf can carry bacteria from an infected quarter or from its mouth to healthy teats.
Tick bites and tick wounds on the teats and udder damage the skin and open the way for infection.
Teat injuries from thorny browse, rough ground, tight teat-tying strings or anti-suckling devices allow bacteria into the teat.
Dirty, wet or muddy resting areas, especially in bomas (night enclosures) during the long and short rains, expose the teats to dung bacteria when the camel lies down.
Flies feeding on milk drops and teat wounds can carry bacteria between camels.
Incomplete milking, where milk is left in the udder for long periods, gives bacteria a place to grow.
detail.atRisk: Any lactating she-camel can get mastitis, but risk is highest in camels in early lactation, older camels that have had many calves, and camels with previous udder problems or damaged teats. Heavy-milking camels in peri-urban and commercial dairy herds, such as around Isiolo, Nanyuki, Garissa and Nairobi, are at high risk because they are milked often and by several people. In pastoral herds in Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Turkana, Samburu and Isiolo, risk rises where teats are tied, where tick loads are heavy, and where water for washing hands and containers is scarce. Wet seasons bring muddy bomas and more dung contamination, while dry seasons bring poor nutrition, weaker immunity and high tick numbers. Camels whose calves have died and are not milked out properly can also develop mastitis.

early: Milk from one teat looks slightly different: a few small flakes, clots or a watery appearance, which you see best when you strip the first squirts onto a dark surface or cloth.
One quarter feels a little firmer, warmer or slightly larger than the others when you compare them by hand.
The camel is restless, kicks or moves away during milking, or refuses to let the calf suckle one particular teat.
Milk yield from the camel drops a little without any other obvious reason.
Small tick bites, cuts, cracks or swellings are seen on or near the teat openings.
In subclinical mastitis there may be no visible sign at all, and only a test such as the California Mastitis Test shows a problem.
advanced: One or more quarters are clearly swollen, hard, hot and painful to touch, and the skin may look tight or reddened.
Milk becomes thick, yellow or brown, full of clots, very watery like whey, or tinged pink or red with blood.
The milk may have a bad or sour smell.
The camel has a fever, stops eating, stands apart from the herd, and may be weak or lie down more than usual.
An abscess (a pocket of pus) may form in the udder, sometimes bursting through the skin.
The quarter becomes shrunken and hard over time and gives little or no milk, a so-called blind quarter.
In severe toxic cases the camel becomes very dull and dehydrated and can die without prompt treatment.

lookalikes.name: Udder or teat injury without infection
lookalikes.howToTell: Bruising from thorns, kicks or tight teat-tying strings causes swelling where the injury is, but the milk usually stays normal and a mastitis test stays negative. If the milk changes or the camel gets a fever, infection has likely set in.

lookalikes.name: Tick infestation and tick abscesses
lookalikes.howToTell: Heavy ticks on the udder cause small hard lumps and sores on the skin, but the inside of the quarter feels soft and milk is normal. Ticks often lead to mastitis, so check both the skin and the milk.

lookalikes.name: Udder swelling (oedema) near calving
lookalikes.howToTell: Around calving the whole udder and the belly in front of it can be swollen and puffy, often evenly on all quarters, and pressing leaves a dent. It is not hot or painful and the milk is normal. Mastitis usually affects one quarter and changes the milk.

lookalikes.name: Camel pox
lookalikes.howToTell: Camel pox causes raised spots and scabs on the lips, nose, head and sometimes the udder and teats, often in young camels and several animals at once. The milk inside may be normal unless bacteria invade the sores.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer first examines the udder, feeling each quarter for heat, hardness and pain, and checks the teats for wounds, ticks and blocked openings. They strip milk from each quarter to look for clots, colour change or blood. The California Mastitis Test (CMT) is a simple, cheap cow-side test: milk from each quarter is mixed with a reagent in a paddle, and the mixture thickens if the milk has many white blood cells, showing hidden infection. It works in camels, though reading the results needs some experience because camel milk behaves a little differently from cow milk. For stubborn or repeated cases, or herd problems, the vet may take clean milk samples into sterile tubes and send them to a laboratory for culture, which identifies the bacteria, and a sensitivity test, which shows which antibiotics will work. Laboratories at county veterinary offices, universities and KALRO centres may offer this. To help, keep a record of which camel and which quarter is affected, when you first noticed it, how much milk she normally gives, any tick problems, and any drugs already given. Do not treat before samples are taken if you can avoid it, because drugs can make the lab test useless.
firstSteps: Separate the affected camel from the milking line and milk her last, so your hands and containers do not carry infection to healthy camels.
Wash your hands with soap and clean water before and after handling her udder, and use a separate container for milk from the sick quarter.
Strip out the affected quarter gently and often if she tolerates it, because removing infected milk helps reduce pressure and the number of bacteria; do not squeeze roughly.
Throw milk from infected quarters away safely by burying it or pouring it in a pit away from people, animals and water sources; do not drink it, sell it or feed it to calves or dogs.
Remove any ticks you can see on the udder by hand with gloves, without crushing them, and keep the camel in a clean, dry, shaded place.
Remove any teat-tying strings or tight anti-suckling devices from the affected camel so the teats can heal.
Make sure she has easy access to clean drinking water and good browse or fodder, especially if she has a fever or is off feed.
Write down the camel, the quarter, the date and the signs, then call your vet or County animal health officer; do not give antibiotics or other drugs unless a vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how severe the mastitis is and which bacteria are involved, and it must be decided and prescribed by a vet. For clinical mastitis, vets commonly use antibiotics, either as intramammary tubes placed into the teat (in camels each teat opening may need attention) or as injections when the camel is generally sick. Commonly used drug groups include penicillins, cloxacillin, cephalosporins, oxytetracycline and some combinations, chosen according to the likely bacteria and, ideally, lab sensitivity results. For a feverish or toxic camel the vet may add an anti-inflammatory painkiller such as flunixin or meloxicam, and fluids. Abscesses may need to be lanced and cleaned. Frequent stripping of the quarter is usually advised. Some badly damaged quarters will not recover and the vet may advise drying off that quarter or, for repeated cases, culling the camel. Every drug used has a milk withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment when milk must be thrown away because it contains drug residues, and many drugs also have a meat withdrawal period. Withdrawal periods for camels are often not on the label, so ask your vet, who usually advises an extended period. Use antibiotics responsibly: give the full course exactly as prescribed, never use leftover tubes or share them between animals without advice, and do not buy antibiotics to treat on guesswork. Misuse leads to antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to drugs, which harms both animals and people.
prevention: Wash hands with soap and clean water before milking, and between camels if possible; keep nails short and cover any cuts on your hands.
Clean and dry the teats before milking with a clean cloth for each camel, or a single-use paper towel, and avoid sharing one wet cloth for the whole herd.

Use clean, smooth containers such as food-grade aluminium or stainless steel cans that are easy to wash, and scald or wash them well after every milking; traditional woven or wooden containers are hard to clean.
Dip or spray the teats with a vet-approved teat disinfectant after milking to kill bacteria at the teat openings.
Milk out each camel fully and in a calm, gentle way, and milk known infected camels last.
Control ticks regularly with an acaricide (tick-killing product) advised by your vet or agrovet, paying special attention to the udder, teats and the area between the hind legs.
Avoid tying teats with string or using tight or thorny anti-suckling devices; if you must restrict suckling, use soft, clean, loose udder covers and check the teats daily for injury.
Keep bomas clean and dry, remove dung regularly, and give camels clean resting ground, especially during the rains.
Test camels with the California Mastitis Test regularly, for example monthly in dairy herds, to find hidden infections early.

Feed well, give access to salt and minerals, and support vitamin intake in the dry season, because well-nourished camels resist infection better; cull camels with repeated mastitis or permanently damaged quarters.
detail.impact: Mastitis is one of the biggest causes of lost camel milk in Kenya. Clinical cases mean milk must be thrown away during illness and treatment withdrawal, and a damaged quarter may never return to full production. Subclinical mastitis is often the larger hidden loss, because many camels quietly give less milk for months without the owner knowing why. Poor-quality milk with high bacteria spoils faster in hot conditions, fetches lower prices and can be rejected by milk traders, cooperatives and processors. Treatment and vet costs add up, calves may get less milk and grow slowly, and valuable milking camels may need to be culled early. For pastoral families who depend on camel milk for daily food, especially in the dry season, these losses directly affect household nutrition and income.
detail.humanHealth: Milk from camels with mastitis can contain large numbers of bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, which can produce toxins that cause food poisoning, and streptococci and E. coli that can make people ill. Camel milk is often drunk raw or fermented, which increases the risk. Raw camel milk can also carry other serious infections such as brucellosis, even from camels that look healthy. Boil or properly pasteurise camel milk before drinking, never drink or sell milk from infected quarters, and keep milk cool and covered. Milk from treated camels contains antibiotic residues that can cause allergic reactions in some people and encourage antimicrobial resistance, so always respect the milk withdrawal period advised by your vet. Wash your hands after handling infected udders and cover any cuts.
detail.outlook: Mild cases caught early, especially those found by regular testing, usually respond well to vet-guided treatment and good milking hygiene, and the quarter often returns to near-normal milk. Severe cases with fever, very hard quarters or abscesses take longer and may leave the quarter permanently damaged or dry. Infections with some Staphylococcus aureus strains can be stubborn and come back, even after treatment. Recovery is more likely when the right drug is chosen, the full course is completed, ticks and teat injuries are controlled, and milking hygiene improves. Camels with repeated mastitis in the same quarters seldom become fully productive again and are often best culled.

faqs.q: Can I still drink milk from the healthy quarters of a camel with mastitis?
faqs.a: If the camel is not being treated with drugs and only one quarter is affected, milk from the healthy quarters can usually be used after boiling, as long as you milk the infected quarter last into a separate container. Once the camel is given antibiotics, especially by injection, all her milk may contain residues, so follow your vet's advice on the withdrawal period before using any milk.

faqs.q: My camel's milk looks normal but her yield has dropped. Could it be mastitis?
faqs.a: Yes. Subclinical mastitis often shows no visible change in the milk or udder, only a drop in yield. Ask your vet or animal health officer to do a California Mastitis Test on each quarter. It is quick and cheap, and it shows hidden infection so you can act before it becomes serious.

faqs.q: Is it safe to tie the teats to stop the calf suckling?
faqs.a: Tying teats with string or using tight or thorny devices is a common practice, but it often damages the teats, traps dirt and milk, and increases mastitis. If you need to limit suckling, use a soft, clean, loose udder cover, remove it regularly, and check the teats every day for cuts or swelling.

faqs.q: Can I buy a mastitis tube from the agrovet and treat my camel myself?
faqs.a: It is better to have a vet or animal health officer examine the camel first. Many mastitis tubes are made for cows, camel teats have more than one opening, and the wrong drug or poor technique can push dirt into the teat or fail to clear the infection. A vet can choose the right treatment, show you how to give it hygienically, and tell you how long to throw away the milk.

faqs.q: Why do ticks matter so much for udder health in camels?
faqs.a: Large ticks often attach on the udder and teats, and their bites cause sores, swelling and damage to the teat openings. Bacteria then enter easily and cause mastitis. Regular tick control, with special attention to the udder area, is one of the most useful ways to prevent mastitis in camel herds.

faqs.q: Should I let the calf suckle the infected quarter to empty it?
faqs.a: It is better not to. The calf can spread bacteria to other teats and to other camels, and the milk is poor for the calf. Strip that quarter by hand into a separate container instead, and let the calf suckle only the healthy quarters while the camel is being treated.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can help a feverish camel that is drinking or eating less to stay hydrated and keep up her strength during recovery, used alongside vet treatment and not as a treatment for the udder infection itself.

A vitamin A, D3 and E supplement that can help correct vitamin shortages common in the dry season when green browse is scarce; vitamins A and E support healthy skin and teat lining and normal immune function, so it supports udder health as part of good nutrition, used as directed by your vet, and does not cure mastitis.

mastitis.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a dromedary camel's udder in a dry northern Kenyan boma, with one quarter clearly more swollen and firmer-looking than the other three and its teat slightly reddened, in natural daylight.
mastitis.seoDescription: Camel mastitis: spot swollen hot udder quarters and abnormal milk, act fast, call the vet, and prevent udder infection with clean milking and tick control.

card.headline: Clusters of large ticks on udder
card.look: You see big, hard-bodied brown ticks, often with banded legs, packed onto the udder, teats, around the tail and vulva, and between the hind legs. Teats may be swollen, scabbed or cracked, and some quarters may give little or no milk.
card.action: Examine every camel's udder, perineum and inner legs today, then call your vet or animal health officer for advice on a camel-safe tick control plan.

detail.summary: Tick infestation means many ticks are attached to a camel and feeding on its blood. In camels the most important ticks belong to the Hyalomma group, and they prefer the soft, thin skin of the udder, teats, perineum (the area around the anus and vulva) and between the legs. Heavy burdens damage teats, open the way for mastitis (infection of the udder), cause blood loss and weakness, and spread germs that cause disease in camels and people. In pastoral herds where milk is the main food and income, this is a serious and often underestimated problem.
detail.cause: Ticks are eight-legged blood-sucking parasites related to spiders. The main camel tick in East Africa is Hyalomma dromedarii. Other Hyalomma species, along with Amblyomma (bont ticks, with colourful shields) and Rhipicephalus species, also feed on camels. Hyalomma ticks have long mouthparts that cut deep into the skin. Each tick feeds for several days, swelling up with blood before dropping off to lay thousands of eggs on the ground, in boma walls or in resting places. When dozens or hundreds of ticks feed at once, the camel loses blood and can become anaemic (short of red blood cells), which shows as weakness and pale gums. The deep bites cause pain, swelling and wounds. On the teats, bites and the swelling that follows can block the teat canal, damage the teat end and let bacteria into the udder, causing mastitis and sometimes permanent loss of a quarter, known as a blind teat. Wounds can become infected, form abscesses, or attract flies that lay eggs in them. Ticks also inject saliva that can carry germs, including Anaplasma and other blood parasites, Coxiella (the cause of Q fever) and the virus that causes Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever in people.
spread: Camels pick up ticks while grazing and browsing in bush and grassland where young ticks wait on vegetation for a passing host.

Hyalomma dromedarii often lives where camels rest, hiding in cracks of boma walls, thorn fences, dung and soil, so camels kept in the same night enclosure for a long time are reinfested again and again.
Mixing with other herds at watering points, markets and shared grazing brings in ticks from other animals, including cattle, goats and wildlife.
Buying or borrowing camels without checking and treating them first introduces new ticks and the diseases they carry onto the farm.
Moving herds into new grazing areas during migration or drought can expose camels to different tick species and heavier tick populations.
Poor or irregular tick control, wrong products, weak dilutions or treating only some animals allows ticks to survive, breed and build up resistance to acaricides (tick-killing chemicals).
detail.atRisk: All camels can carry ticks, but lactating she-camels suffer most because ticks cluster on the udder and teats, directly threatening milk supply and calf feeding. Young calves, old camels, and animals already weakened by poor feeding, worms, trypanosomiasis (surra) or recent illness cope worst with blood loss. Herds in northern and eastern Kenya, such as Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Turkana and Laikipia, live where camel ticks are common. Tick numbers often rise during and after the long and short rains when vegetation is lush, but Hyalomma ticks tolerate heat and dryness well and can remain a problem in the dry season too; patterns vary by area. Herds kept in the same boma for long periods, herds that share watering points, and herds where tick checks are not routine carry the heaviest burdens.

early: A few to several ticks attached under the tail, around the anus and vulva, on the udder, teats, inner thighs, armpits, belly or brisket.
The camel rubs its hindquarters against trees or fences, kicks at its belly or swishes its tail more than usual.
Small raised, tender bumps or scabs where ticks have been attached and dropped off.
Slight swelling or redness of the teats, and the camel may resist milking or kick when the udder is touched.
Calves may be pushed away at suckling because the teats are sore.
advanced: Dense clusters of large engorged ticks, some the size of a bean or larger, crowded on the udder, teats and perineum.
Swollen, hot, hard quarters with clots, flakes, watery or bloody milk, showing mastitis.
Teats with deep cracks, scabs, abscesses or a teat that gives no milk at all (blind quarter).
Pale pink or whitish gums and inner eyelids, weakness, lagging behind the herd and loss of body condition from blood loss.
Infected wounds with pus, a bad smell or fly maggots in them.
Fever, dullness, reduced feeding, drop in milk yield, or abortion, which may point to a tick-borne infection and needs a vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: Mange (Sarcoptic mange, 'scabies')
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange is caused by tiny mites you cannot see. The camel itches intensely, with hair loss, thick crusty or wrinkled skin often starting on the head, neck, flanks and inner legs. You will not find large attached ticks; a vet confirms mange with a skin scraping.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (surra)
lookalikes.howToTell: Surra, spread by biting flies, also causes anaemia, weakness and weight loss, sometimes with swelling under the belly and abortion. Anaemia with few ticks on the body suggests surra or worms rather than ticks. A vet confirms it with a blood test.

lookalikes.name: Camel keds (Hippobosca flies)
lookalikes.howToTell: Keds are flat, brownish flies that crawl quickly through the hair around the tail and belly and can fly off. Ticks are round, firmly attached, and do not move away when touched.

lookalikes.name: Mastitis from other causes
lookalikes.howToTell: Udder infection can follow poor milking hygiene, injury or calf bites without ticks. If the udder is hot and milk is abnormal but there are no ticks or bite wounds on the teats, other causes are likely, though ticks may still have been involved earlier.

detail.diagnosis: Diagnosing the infestation itself is simple: a careful look at the udder, teats, perineum, under the tail, inner thighs, armpits, ears and belly. The vet will judge how heavy the burden is and look for damage: teat wounds, abscesses, mastitis and signs of anaemia such as pale gums. To identify the tick species, which helps choose control methods and judge disease risk, the vet may collect ticks for a county veterinary laboratory or KALRO. A blood sample can measure anaemia (packed cell volume) and be checked for blood parasites such as Anaplasma or trypanosomes. For mastitis, the vet may do a California Mastitis Test at the camel side and send milk for culture to find which bacteria are involved and which antibiotics will work. You can prepare by penning the affected camels, noting which animals are worst, how long the problem has been building, any drop in milk, which tick products you have used before with dates and dilutions, and by collecting a few ticks in a small jar or bottle with spirit, without crushing them with bare hands.
firstSteps: Restrain the camel calmly and inspect every animal in the herd, paying close attention to the udder, teats, perineum, under the tail and between the legs.
Wear gloves or use a cloth or tweezers if you remove ticks by hand, and never crush ticks with fingers, nails or teeth because their contents can infect people.
When removing a tick, grip it close to the skin and pull steadily straight out rather than twisting or tearing, because Hyalomma mouthparts left in the skin cause abscesses.
Drop removed ticks into a container with spirit or burn them, instead of throwing them on the ground where engorged females will lay eggs.
Do not apply used engine oil, paraffin, battery acid or other harsh home remedies to the udder, as they burn the skin, contaminate the milk and can poison the camel.
Milk sore or swollen quarters gently and completely, keep the udder clean, and separate milk from quarters with clots, blood or watery milk so it is not drunk or sold.
Give plenty of clean water, shade and good browse, and keep weak or pale camels from long treks until they are assessed.
Record which camels are affected, milk yield changes and any fever or dullness, then call your vet or animal health officer before using any acaricide or medicine.
detail.vetTreatment: The vet will plan two things: killing the ticks now, and treating the damage they have caused. For the ticks, the main options are acaricides such as synthetic pyrethroids (for example deltamethrin, cypermethrin or flumethrin as sprays or pour-ons), amitraz, or organophosphates, and sometimes macrocyclic lactones such as ivermectin, which have only a partial effect on ticks. Many of these products are made for cattle and are not specifically licensed for camels, and camels can react badly to some chemicals or wrong dilutions, so the vet must choose the product, method and interval. Hand-spraying or applying the product carefully to the udder, perineum and legs is often needed because these hidden areas are where ticks hide. The vet may also advise treating the boma and resting places. Damaged teats and wounds are cleaned and may be dressed. Mastitis is treated according to the vet's examination and, ideally, milk culture, sometimes with intramammary tubes (inserted into the teat) or injectable antibiotics. Antibiotics must only be used when the vet prescribes them and the full course must be completed, because misuse breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance) that threaten both animal and human health. Anaemic camels need rest, good feeding and checks for worms and trypanosomes, and very severe cases may need extra supportive care. Every acaricide and antibiotic has a milk and meat withdrawal period, the time during which milk and meat must not be used. For camels these periods are often not well established, so the vet will advise a safe, usually cautious, withdrawal time. Expect ticks to die within days of correct treatment, but new ticks will keep arriving, so repeat treatment on a schedule is usually needed. Teat damage and mastitis may take weeks to settle and some quarters may not recover.
prevention: Check camels at least weekly, and more often during and after the rains, especially the udder, teats, perineum, under the tail, inner thighs and armpits, and remove or treat ticks early before burdens build up.

Work with your vet or animal health officer on a strategic tick control plan using a camel-appropriate acaricide at the right dilution and interval, treating the whole herd, not just the worst animals.
Follow product directions exactly: weak mixtures, skipped animals and frequent switching of products help ticks survive and become resistant.
Clean bomas regularly, remove built-up dung and bedding, seal or treat cracks in walls where Hyalomma ticks hide, and move the night enclosure to a fresh site when practical.
Quarantine new or returning camels for a period, inspect them closely and treat them before they join the herd.
Limit contact with heavily infested herds at shared watering points and markets where possible, and inspect camels after such visits.
Keep good milking hygiene: wash and dry hands and teats, milk completely, watch every quarter for clots or swelling, and deal with teat wounds quickly.
Keep camels in good body condition with adequate browse, water and minerals, and control worms and trypanosomiasis so camels can better withstand blood loss from ticks.
detail.impact: For pastoral families, camel milk is food for children and a key source of cash, so ticks on the udder hit directly where it matters most. Sore teats lead to reduced milk let-down, refusal to be milked and poor calf feeding. Mastitis lowers milk yield and quality, milk must be discarded during treatment and withdrawal periods, and blind quarters can permanently reduce a she-camel's production for the rest of her life. Calves on damaged udders grow slowly or may need extra feeding. Anaemia and constant irritation reduce body condition, fertility and the camel's ability to walk long distances to water and grazing. Damaged hides lose value, and tick-borne infections can cause illness, abortion and occasionally deaths. Add the cost of acaricides, vet visits and labour, and repeated heavy tick burdens become an important drain on herd income.
detail.humanHealth: Ticks on camels can carry germs that infect people. The most serious is Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), a viral disease spread mainly by Hyalomma ticks. Camels usually show no sign of this virus but can carry it and feed infected ticks. People can be infected by a tick bite, by crushing ticks with bare hands, or by contact with blood and tissues of infected animals at slaughter. Camel ticks can also carry Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) and rickettsia that cause tick-bite fever. To protect yourself: wear gloves when removing ticks, never crush them with fingers or teeth, wash hands with soap after handling camels, check your own body and clothes after herding, and seek medical care quickly if you get sudden fever, headache, muscle pain or unusual bleeding after a tick bite or handling livestock. Acaricides are poisons: wear gloves and protective clothing when mixing and applying them, keep them away from children, food and water, and do not drink or sell milk or meat before the withdrawal period your vet gives has passed.
detail.outlook: The outlook for tick infestation itself is good when it is caught early and treated correctly: ticks can be killed and burdens kept low with regular checks and a sound control plan. The outlook becomes more guarded once complications appear. Mild teat wounds usually heal, but deep damage, abscesses and chronic mastitis can leave a quarter permanently blind. Badly anaemic or thin camels recover more slowly and need good feeding and rest. Tick-borne infections can complicate recovery and need a vet's diagnosis. Because ticks keep returning from the environment and other herds, long-term success depends on steady, whole-herd prevention rather than one-off treatment.

faqs.q: Can I use the same cattle dip or spray on my camels?
faqs.a: Some acaricides used on cattle are also used on camels, but camels can react differently and many products are not labelled for camels. The dilution, method and interval matter a lot. Ask your vet or animal health officer which product is suitable and how to apply it to the hidden areas like the udder and perineum. Never guess the strength.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from a camel I have just sprayed for ticks?
faqs.a: Not until the withdrawal period has passed. Acaricides can pass into milk, and camel milk is often drunk raw, especially by children. Withdrawal times for camels are often not well known, so follow your vet's advice, which is usually cautious, and discard or keep aside milk during that time.

faqs.q: Is hand-picking ticks a good idea?
faqs.a: Hand-picking is a long tradition in camel herds and helps, especially on the udder, but it must be done safely. Wear gloves, pull ticks straight out close to the skin, do not crush them, and destroy them in spirit or fire. On its own, hand-picking rarely keeps up with heavy infestations, so combine it with a vet-advised acaricide plan and boma cleaning.

faqs.q: Why do the ticks come back so quickly after I treat?
faqs.a: Treatment kills ticks on the camel but not the eggs and young ticks waiting in the boma walls, dung and grazing land. New ticks attach within days. Ticks may also be resistant if the same product has been used wrongly for years. Treat the whole herd on a regular schedule, clean and treat resting places, and ask your vet to check whether resistance is a problem.

faqs.q: Can ticks really make a teat stop giving milk?
faqs.a: Yes. Deep Hyalomma bites cause swelling and wounds on the teat. Bacteria can enter and cause mastitis, and scarring can block the teat canal so that quarter gives little or no milk. Early tick control and quick care of teat wounds and mastitis give the best chance of saving the quarter.

faqs.q: My camel is weak with pale gums but has few ticks. Is it still ticks?
faqs.a: Possibly not. Pale gums and weakness with only a few ticks point to other causes such as trypanosomiasis (surra), worms or a tick-borne blood parasite. Ask your vet for a blood test so the right cause is treated.

tick-infestation.imagePrompt: Close-up photograph of a dromedary camel's udder and teats in a dry Kenyan boma, with several large brown banded-leg Hyalomma ticks clustered on the teats and udder skin, natural daylight, no people.
tick-infestation.seoDescription: Tick infestation in camels: spot Hyalomma ticks on udder and perineum, prevent teat damage, mastitis and anaemia, and know when to call the vet in Kenya.

card.headline: Watery scours and soiled tail in calves
card.look: A young camel calf, usually under about three months old, passes watery yellow, green or grey dung that stains its tail and hind legs. It stops suckling, looks weak, and its eyes may look sunken.
card.action: Separate the sick calf into a clean, shaded pen, keep it drinking fluids and suckling, and call your vet or animal health worker the same day.

detail.summary: Camel calf diarrhoea, often called scours, is a common and serious problem in young camel calves, mostly in the first weeks of life. Germs such as E. coli, rotavirus and Salmonella damage the gut, so the calf loses large amounts of water and salts in its dung. A calf can become badly dehydrated within a day or two, and it is one of the main causes of calf deaths in camel herds in northern Kenya and the wider Horn of Africa. Good colostrum feeding and clean calf pens prevent many cases.
detail.cause: Scours in camel calves is usually caused by germs, often more than one at the same time. The main ones are bacteria such as E. coli (especially in the first days of life) and Salmonella, viruses such as rotavirus and coronavirus, and tiny parasites such as Cryptosporidium. In older calves, coccidia (another gut parasite) and worms can also cause diarrhoea. These germs attack the lining of the small intestine. Some bacteria make toxins that force the gut to pour out water and salts; viruses and parasites destroy the small finger-like structures (villi) that absorb milk, so milk passes through undigested. The result is watery dung, loss of body water and important salts such as sodium and potassium, and a build-up of acid in the blood. This is what makes the calf weak, cold and unable to stand, and it is the dehydration, more than the germ itself, that usually kills. Salmonella and some E. coli can also enter the bloodstream and cause blood poisoning (septicaemia). A key reason camel calves are so vulnerable is that they are born with almost no protective antibodies; they get all their early immunity from colostrum, the first thick milk from the dam. If the calf does not get enough good colostrum soon after birth, it has little defence against these germs.
spread: Calves swallow germs from dung of sick calves or carrier adults that contaminates the ground, bedding, water containers and the dam's udder.
Crowded, muddy or dung-filled calf enclosures and night bomas build up very high numbers of germs, especially when the same pen is used season after season.
Poor colostrum intake is a major trigger: calves that suckle late, or whose dam's colostrum is milked off or discarded, have weak immunity and fall sick easily.
Dirty hands, milking containers and feeding utensils carry germs from one calf to the next when people handle many calves.
Stress from cold nights, heavy rain, long treks to water or grazing, dust, heat and sudden changes in milk supply lowers the calf's resistance.
New animals brought into the herd, or mixing with other herds at watering points and markets, can introduce new strains of germs.
Dams that are thin or poorly fed in late pregnancy, for example during drought, often produce less and lower-quality colostrum.
detail.atRisk: Calves in the first few weeks of life are at highest risk, with E. coli scours often seen in the first days and viral and Cryptosporidium scours a little later in the first weeks. Coccidiosis and worm-related diarrhoea are more common in calves a month old or older. Calves that were weak at birth, born to first-time or thin dams, or that did not suckle well in the first hours are much more likely to fall ill. Risk rises when many calves are born close together and kept in the same small enclosure, so problems often show up in the main calving season. The long and short rains bring mud and wet bedding that help germs survive, while drought brings poor dam nutrition, low milk and long walks. Pastoral herds in Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu and Laikipia face particular difficulty because veterinary help may be far away, while peri-urban and semi-intensive camel dairies can see outbreaks when calves are crowded together and milk is heavily taken for sale.

early: Dung becomes soft, then watery, often yellow, pale grey or greenish, and may smell sour or foul.
The tail, hind legs and the area under the tail are wet and stained with dung.
The calf suckles less, leaves the dam early, or shows little interest in milk.
The calf is quieter than usual, stands with a hunched back, or lies down more than other calves.
Mild belly discomfort, such as kicking at the belly, straining or lying and getting up often.
advanced: Sunken eyes and a dry, sticky mouth and gums, which are clear signs of dehydration.
When you pinch and lift the skin on the neck, it stays tented for more than a couple of seconds instead of springing back.
The calf cannot stand or stands only with help, and its legs, ears and mouth feel cold.
Dung may contain mucus or blood, especially with Salmonella or coccidia, and may smell very bad.
The calf stops suckling completely, becomes floppy and dull, and may lie flat on its side.
Fast or very weak breathing, and sometimes high fever early on with Salmonella, followed by a low temperature as the calf goes into shock.
Death, sometimes within a day or two of the first signs in very young calves.

lookalikes.name: Nutritional (milk) diarrhoea
lookalikes.howToTell: This happens after sudden changes in milk supply, such as a calf gorging after a long separation from its dam, or being fed milk replacer or cow milk wrongly. Dung is soft and pasty rather than very watery, the calf stays bright and keeps suckling, and it usually settles within a day or two once feeding is made regular. If the calf becomes dull or dehydrated, treat it as infectious scours.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Usually affects calves older than about three to four weeks rather than newborns. Dung often contains mucus and streaks of fresh blood, and the calf strains a lot. It tends to appear when calves are kept on dirty, damp ground. A vet confirms it by finding coccidia eggs (oocysts) in a dung sample.

lookalikes.name: Worm infestation
lookalikes.howToTell: Seen in older calves that have started grazing. Diarrhoea is more gradual, and the calf loses condition, has a rough coat, a pot belly and pale gums from anaemia. It rarely causes the sudden severe dehydration seen in young calves with scours.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (clostridial disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by Clostridium bacteria toxins, often in well-fed, fast-growing calves. Calves may die very suddenly, sometimes before much diarrhoea is seen, or show bloating, severe belly pain and nervous signs. A post-mortem by a vet is usually needed to tell it apart.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or trained animal health worker first examines the calf: checking body temperature, how sunken the eyes are, the skin tent test, mouth moisture, suck reflex and whether the calf can stand, to judge how dehydrated it is. They will also check the navel for infection and the joints for swelling, which can point to blood poisoning. Because many germs cause the same signs, the exact cause can only be confirmed in a laboratory. The vet may take fresh dung samples for rapid tests (for example for rotavirus or Cryptosporidium), microscope checks for parasites and coccidia, and bacterial culture for E. coli and Salmonella, which also shows which antibiotics will work. Samples can be sent through the County Veterinary Office to regional veterinary laboratories or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. A blood test may show whether the calf received enough colostrum. If a calf dies, a post-mortem examination done quickly is very useful for finding the cause and protecting the rest of the calves. To help, the farmer should note each calf's age, when signs started, colour and smell of the dung, whether it suckled colostrum and how soon, how many calves are sick or have died, and any treatments given. Keep a fresh dung sample in a clean, closed container in a cool place if the vet asks for one, and do not bury a dead calf before the vet has advised.
firstSteps: Move the sick calf, ideally with its dam, into a clean, dry, shaded pen away from healthy calves, and protect it from cold wind at night and strong sun by day.
Let the calf keep suckling its dam or keep feeding its normal milk in small, frequent amounts; do not starve the calf, because milk gives it energy and helps the gut heal.
Give an oral rehydration solution between milk feeds, following the product label or your vet's advice, to replace the water and salts lost in the diarrhoea.
If the calf cannot stand, cannot suck, feels cold, or has very sunken eyes, call the vet urgently; such a calf may need fluids by drip that only a vet can give.
Wear gloves or wash your hands with soap and water after handling the calf or its dung, and keep children away from sick calves.
Clean up dung, burn or bury soiled bedding, and use separate buckets and containers for sick and healthy calves.
Do not give antibiotics, human medicines or leftover drugs without a vet's advice, because the wrong drug can harm the calf and help germs become resistant.
Write down which calves are sick, their ages, when signs started and any deaths, and share this with your vet or County Veterinary Officer.
detail.vetTreatment: The most important part of treatment is replacing lost fluid and salts. For mildly to moderately dehydrated calves that can still suck, the vet will usually advise oral rehydration fluids given between milk feeds, while the calf continues to drink milk. Badly dehydrated, weak or collapsed calves usually need fluids given into a vein (intravenous drip), which must be done by a vet; these fluids also correct the acid build-up in the blood. The vet may give anti-inflammatory pain relief to help the calf feel better and suck again, and will keep the calf warm. Antibiotics are not needed for every case. Viral and Cryptosporidium scours do not respond to antibiotics, because antibiotics do not kill viruses or these parasites. The vet will consider antibiotics mainly when there are signs of blood poisoning, high fever, blood in the dung or suspected Salmonella or severe E. coli infection, and ideally will choose the drug based on laboratory culture and sensitivity results. Using antibiotics only when needed, at the right drug and for the full course the vet prescribes, helps prevent antimicrobial resistance, which is when germs stop responding to medicines that people and animals depend on. If coccidiosis is confirmed, the vet may prescribe an anticoccidial medicine such as a sulphonamide or toltrazuril-type drug; for worms in older calves, a suitable dewormer. All treatment must be prescribed and dosed by a vet, as camels respond differently to some drugs than cattle. If the dam is also treated, ask about the milk withdrawal period (the time milk must be thrown away after treatment so drug residues do not reach people), and meat withdrawal periods apply to any treated animal before slaughter. With early care many calves improve within a few days, but very weak calves can still die despite treatment.
prevention: Make sure every calf suckles colostrum as soon as possible after birth, ideally within the first hour or two, and gets plenty during the first day; do not milk off or throw away the dam's first milk.
Help weak calves to stand and suckle, or milk the dam's colostrum into a clean container and feed it, so that no calf misses this vital first protection.
Feed pregnant dams as well as possible in late pregnancy, including mineral licks and access to browse, so they produce good colostrum and strong calves; seek advice on vitamin support in drought.
Keep calving and calf pens clean and dry: remove dung regularly, move or rest night enclosures, avoid muddy areas, and give calves shade and shelter from cold wind.
Avoid crowding many young calves together, and keep newborn calves apart from older calves that may be shedding germs.
Clean the navel of newborn calves as advised by your vet, and keep the dam's udder and teats free of caked dung.
Wash hands and milking containers, use separate equipment for sick calves, and keep watering troughs clean.

Isolate newly bought or returning animals for a period, and ask your vet whether vaccines or other herd programmes are suitable for your area; there is no widely used camel-specific scours vaccine, so management is the main protection.
Do not take so much milk for sale or home use that young calves go hungry; leave enough milk for the calf to grow and stay strong.
detail.impact: Calf diarrhoea is one of the biggest causes of calf losses in camel herds. Because a camel dam usually gives birth only about every two years, each calf lost is a big setback to herd growth and future income. Calves that survive may grow slowly and reach breeding or market age later. For many pastoral families, camel milk is the main food and source of cash, and some dams may dry off or produce less milk if their calf dies, as camels often need the calf present to let down milk. There are also costs for vet visits, drugs, fluids and labour, and time taken from herding and other work. In camel dairies near towns such as Isiolo, Garissa and Nanyuki, outbreaks can affect many calves at once and reduce milk supply to buyers.
detail.humanHealth: Some of the germs that cause scours, especially Salmonella, certain types of E. coli and Cryptosporidium, can also make people sick with diarrhoea, stomach pain and fever. Children, elderly people, pregnant women and people with weak immunity are most at risk. Always wash hands well with soap and clean water after handling sick calves, their dung or bedding, and before eating or preparing food. Keep children from playing with or kissing sick calves. Boiling or pasteurising camel milk before drinking reduces the risk of picking up these germs, and milk from dams being treated with drugs should be discarded for the withdrawal period the vet gives.
detail.outlook: Calves with mild diarrhoea that keep suckling and get oral fluids early usually recover within several days. The outlook becomes much worse once a calf is severely dehydrated, cold, cannot stand or has stopped sucking, and very young calves that missed colostrum are most likely to die. Salmonella and blood poisoning carry a higher risk of death than simple viral scours. Calves that recover may have reduced growth for a while and need good milk and care. Quick action, good colostrum and clean pens make the biggest difference to survival.

faqs.q: Should I stop giving milk to a calf with diarrhoea?
faqs.a: No. The old practice of starving a scouring calf is not recommended. Milk gives the calf energy and helps the gut repair itself. Let the calf continue to suckle or feed its normal milk in small, frequent amounts, and give oral rehydration fluids separately between feeds, as your vet advises.

faqs.q: Is it true that the first milk (colostrum) is bad for the calf?
faqs.a: No. In some communities colostrum is milked off or thrown away, but it is the calf's most important protection. Camel calves are born with almost no antibodies and depend on colostrum to fight germs. Calves that get plenty of colostrum early are much less likely to get scours or die from it.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and give it?
faqs.a: It is better not to without a vet's advice. Many cases are caused by viruses or parasites that antibiotics cannot kill, and dehydration, not the germ, is usually what kills the calf. Using the wrong drug wastes money, can harm the calf and helps germs become resistant. Let a vet decide if an antibiotic is needed and which one.

faqs.q: How do I know if my calf is dangerously dehydrated?
faqs.a: Look for sunken eyes, a dry or cold mouth, and skin on the neck that stays tented for more than a couple of seconds after you pinch it. A calf that cannot stand, will not suck or feels cold is in danger and needs a vet urgently, as it may need fluids into the vein.

faqs.q: Many of my calves are getting sick at once. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer so samples can be taken to find the cause. Separate sick calves, clean or move the calf enclosure, stop crowding, and make sure all new calves get colostrum quickly. Keep records of ages, signs and deaths to help the vet.

faqs.q: Can I catch diarrhoea from my sick calves?
faqs.a: Yes, some of the germs, such as Salmonella and Cryptosporidium, can infect people. Wash hands with soap after handling calves or dung, keep children away from sick calves, and boil camel milk before drinking to reduce the risk.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that helps replace the water and salts a scouring calf loses in its dung; give it between milk feeds as directed on the label or by your vet, as support alongside veterinary care, not as a cure for the infection.

Vitamins A, D3 and E can help correct deficiencies in pregnant dams and weak calves, especially in drought when dry forage is low in vitamin A, supporting colostrum quality and the calf's natural resistance; use under vet or agrovet guidance as part of good nutrition, not as a treatment for scours.
